items.label: High-yield
items.text: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect).
items.back: what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect).
items.cloze: PK = {{c1::what the body does to the drug (ADME)}}; PD = {{c2::what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect)}}.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: ADR = unintended, harmful, at normal therapeutic doses; toxicity = dose/exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
items.back: unintended, harmful, at normal therapeutic doses; toxicity = dose/exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
items.cloze: ADR = unintended, harmful, at {{c1::normal therapeutic doses}}; toxicity = dose/exposure {{c2::exceeds the therapeutic range}}.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Learn, prescribe, and counsel by generic name — brand names can hide a shared ingredient → double-dosing.
items.front: Learn, prescribe, and counsel by generic name …

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Pharmacology connects a drug's chemistry to its clinical effect.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Pharmacology: the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.
items.back: the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.
items.cloze: {{c1::Pharmacology}}: the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Drug (medication): any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.
items.back: any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.
items.cloze: {{c1::Drug (medication)}}: any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Pharmacologic effect: a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).
items.back: a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).
items.cloze: {{c1::Pharmacologic effect}}: a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).

items.label: Definition
items.text: Therapeutic effect: the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.
items.back: the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.
items.cloze: {{c1::Therapeutic effect}}: the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Adverse drug reaction (ADR): an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.
items.back: an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.
items.cloze: {{c1::Adverse drug reaction (ADR)}}: an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Toxicity: harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
items.back: harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
items.cloze: {{c1::Toxicity}}: harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Chemical name: describes the exact molecular structure (rarely used in clinical practice).
items.back: describes the exact molecular structure (rarely used in clinical practice).
items.cloze: {{c1::Chemical name}}: describes the exact molecular structure (rarely used in clinical practice).

items.label: Definition
items.text: Generic name: the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.
items.back: the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.
items.cloze: {{c1::Generic name}}: the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Brand (trade) name: the manufacturer's marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.
items.back: the manufacturer's marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.
items.cloze: {{c1::Brand (trade) name}}: the manufacturer's marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Prodrug: an inactive precursor converted to the active drug in the body (usually by metabolism).
items.back: an inactive precursor converted to the active drug in the body (usually by metabolism).
items.cloze: {{c1::Prodrug}}: an inactive precursor converted to the active drug in the body (usually by metabolism).

items.label: Definition
items.text: Poisons are drugs with almost exclusively harmful effects — but "the dose makes the poison" (Paracelsus): any substance can harm at the wrong dose.
items.front: Poisons are drugs with almost exclusively harmful effects …
items.back: but "the dose makes the poison" (Paracelsus): any substance can harm at the wrong dose.
items.cloze: {{c1::Poisons}} are drugs with almost exclusively harmful effects — but "the dose makes the poison" (Paracelsus): any substance can harm at the wrong dose.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: PA students should learn and prescribe by generic name — it is unambiguous, international, and avoids confusing a patient's multiple brand-name products for different drugs.
items.front: PA students should learn and prescribe by generic name …
items.back: it is unambiguous, international, and avoids confusing a patient's multiple brand-name products for different drugs.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient.
items.cloze: Different brand-name products ({{c1::Tylenol}}, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: If a patient says they take "Tylenol" and separately "acetaminophen," check for accidental double-dosing — this previews the acetaminophen toxicity discussion.
items.cloze: If a patient says they take "{{c1::Tylenol}}" and separately "acetaminophen," check for accidental double-dosing — this previews the acetaminophen toxicity discussion.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Precise vocabulary (generic names, therapeutic vs. adverse effects) protects patients.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: More than half of prescriptions in the USA are for generic drugs.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Weak bonds need a precise fit, so they are more selective. Aspirin’s covalent bond to platelet cyclooxygenase lasts until new platelets are made.
items.cloze: Weak bonds need a precise fit, so they are {{c1::more selective}}. Aspirin’s covalent bond to platelet cyclooxygenase lasts until new platelets are made.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: "Therapeutic effect" and "pharmacologic effect" are not synonyms — a drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic (that is often exactly what an adverse effect is).
items.front: "Therapeutic effect" and "pharmacologic effect" are not synonyms …
items.back: a drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic (that is often exactly what an adverse effect is).

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: ADR vs. toxicity: an ADR happens at normal therapeutic doses; toxicity happens when dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
items.back: an ADR happens at normal therapeutic doses; toxicity happens when dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
items.cloze: ADR vs. toxicity: {{c1::an ADR happens at normal therapeutic doses}}; toxicity happens when dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Generic names do NOT vary by manufacturer (one per drug); brand names DO vary — and change between countries.
items.cloze: Generic names do NOT vary by manufacturer (one per drug); brand names DO vary — {{c1::and change between countries}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug — ADME.
items.back: what the body does to the drug — ADME.
items.cloze: Pharmacokinetics = {{c1::what the body does to the drug — ADME}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body — receptors & effect.
items.back: what the drug does to the body — receptors & effect.
items.cloze: Pharmacodynamics = {{c1::what the drug does to the body — receptors & effect}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Pharmacogenomics = how genetic variation shapes individual drug response.
items.back: how genetic variation shapes individual drug response.
items.cloze: Pharmacogenomics = {{c1::how genetic variation shapes individual drug response}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Clinical Pharmacology / Toxicology = applying PK/PD to real patients, and the study of poisoning.
items.back: applying PK/PD to real patients, and the study of poisoning.
items.cloze: Clinical Pharmacology / Toxicology = {{c1::applying PK/PD to real patients, and the study of poisoning}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: This map covers the whole lecture: PK and PD are the two biggest buckets, and nearly everything else (toxicology, pharmacogenomics, therapeutics) sits on top of them.

items.back: PK and PD are the two biggest buckets, and nearly everything else (toxicology, pharmacogenomics, therapeutics) sits on top of them.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Drugs bind receptors by covalent bonds (strong, often irreversible), electrostatic bonds (most common) or hydrophobic bonds (weak).
items.cloze: Drugs bind receptors by {{c1::covalent}} bonds (strong, often irreversible), {{c2::electrostatic}} bonds (most common) or {{c3::hydrophobic}} bonds (weak).

items.label: How it works
items.text: Chirality: over half of drugs are mirror-image pairs (enantiomers); one is usually much more potent, yet most are sold as 50:50 mixtures.
items.back: over half of drugs are mirror-image pairs (enantiomers); one is usually much more potent, yet most are sold as 50:50 mixtures.
items.cloze: {{c1::Chirality}}: over half of drugs are mirror-image pairs (enantiomers); one is usually much more potent, yet most are sold as 50:50 mixtures.

items.label: Example
items.text: Acetaminophen (generic) is sold as Tylenol and under many store brands.
items.cloze: {{c1::Acetaminophen}} (generic) is sold as {{c2::Tylenol}} and under many store brands.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why prescribe by generic name? One drug has ONE generic name but can hide under SEVERAL brand names — so brand-name products can conceal duplicate therapy and cause double-dosing.
items.back: One drug has ONE generic name but can hide under SEVERAL brand names — so brand-name products can conceal duplicate therapy and cause double-dosing.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: PharmacoKinetics = the body Keeps the drug moving (ADME). PharmacoDynamics = what the Drug Does to the body.
items.back: the body Keeps the drug moving (ADME). PharmacoDynamics = what the Drug Does to the body.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: ADR = At normal Doses, Reaction is harmful. Toxicity = Too much (exceeds the therapeutic range).
items.back: At normal Doses, Reaction is harmful. Toxicity = Too much (exceeds the therapeutic range).

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Efficacy = ideal trial conditions; effectiveness = everyday practice (adherence, comorbidities).
items.back: ideal trial conditions; effectiveness = everyday practice (adherence, comorbidities).
items.cloze: {{c1::Efficacy}} = ideal trial conditions; {{c2::effectiveness}} = everyday practice (adherence, comorbidities).

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Phase I healthy volunteers → II few hundred patients → III hundreds–thousands (confirm) → IV postmarketing.
items.back: II few hundred patients → III hundreds–thousands (confirm) → IV postmarketing.
items.cloze: Phase I healthy volunteers → {{c1::II few hundred patients → III hundreds–thousands (confirm) → IV postmarketing}}.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Rare adverse effects (1 in 10,000) are often first found in Phase IV.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Risk-benefit is always comparative — ask "compared to what?"
items.cloze: Risk-benefit is always comparative … {{c1::ask "compared to what?"}}

items.label: Definition
items.text: Efficacy: how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.
items.back: how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.
items.cloze: {{c1::Efficacy}}: how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Effectiveness: how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.
items.back: how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.
items.cloze: {{c1::Effectiveness}}: how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Drug interactions can also reduce real-world effectiveness below trial efficacy.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Benefit vs. risk: the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.
items.back: the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.
items.cloze: {{c1::Benefit vs. risk}}: the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Adverse-event reporting: ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.
items.back: ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.
items.cloze: {{c1::Adverse-event reporting}}: ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Double-blind: neither subjects nor evaluators know who gets drug or placebo. Crossover: each subject gets every treatment in turn.
items.back: neither subjects nor evaluators know who gets drug or placebo. Crossover: each subject gets every treatment in turn.
items.cloze: {{c1::Double-blind}}: neither subjects nor evaluators know who gets drug or placebo. {{c2::Crossover}}: each subject gets every treatment in turn.

items.label: Definition
items.text: IRB: the committee at each trial site that approves the ethics of the study; participants give informed consent.
items.back: the committee at each trial site that approves the ethics of the study; participants give informed consent.
items.cloze: {{c1::IRB}}: the committee at each trial site that approves the ethics of the study; participants give informed consent.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Postmarketing surveillance (Phase IV) is where rare adverse effects are often first detected — trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Case: a new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition, but postmarketing data show serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?
items.back: a new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition, but postmarketing data show serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?
items.cloze: Case: a new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition, but postmarketing data show serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. {{c1::Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?}}

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Clinical pearl: risk-benefit analysis is always comparative — a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.
items.back: risk-benefit analysis is always comparative — a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.
items.cloze: {{c1::Clinical pearl}}: risk-benefit analysis is always comparative — a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Ask "compared to what?" rather than judging the number in isolation.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: A patent lasts 20 years; after it expires, generics are approved through an abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) that requires bioequivalence data.
items.cloze: A patent lasts 20 years; after it expires, generics are approved through an {{c1::abbreviated new drug application (ANDA)}} that requires bioequivalence data.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Placebo responses can occur in as many as 30–40% of subjects — the reason controlled, blinded trials are needed.
items.front: Placebo responses can occur in as many as 30–40% of subjects …
items.back: the reason controlled, blinded trials are needed.
items.cloze: Placebo responses can occur in as many as 30–40% of subjects … {{c1::the reason controlled, blinded trials are needed}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Adverse events that are both serious and unexpected must be reported to the FDA within 15 days; clinicians can report through MedWatch.
items.cloze: Adverse events that are both {{c1::serious and unexpected}} must be reported to the FDA within 15 days; clinicians can report through MedWatch.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Dietary supplements are regulated as food under DSHEA (1994), so they get no full FDA drug review.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction: efficacy is the trial result; effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.
items.front: Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction
items.back: efficacy is the trial result; effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.
items.cloze: Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction: {{c1::efficacy is the trial result}}; effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Phase III — not Phase I, II, or IV — is the large pre-approval trial that confirms efficacy and monitors safety at scale.
items.back: not Phase I, II, or IV — is the large pre-approval trial that confirms efficacy and monitors safety at scale.
items.cloze: Phase III — {{c1::not Phase I, II, or IV — is the large pre-approval trial that confirms efficacy and monitors safety at scale}}.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Phase III is what most people picture as "the" clinical trial, but regulatory decisions already begin shaping the drug long before that.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Where new drugs come from — Natural products: plants, fungi, microbes, marine organisms.
items.front: Where new drugs come from — Natural products
items.cloze: Where new drugs come from — Natural products: {{c1::plants, fungi, microbes, marine organisms}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Synthetic & biotech: designed small molecules; recombinant proteins.
items.cloze: Synthetic & biotech: {{c1::designed small molecules}}; recombinant proteins.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Biologics: monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.
items.back: monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.
items.cloze: Biologics: {{c1::monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Drug repurposing: an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.
items.back: an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.
items.cloze: Drug repurposing: {{c1::an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: From discovery to patient: Discovery → Preclinical testing → Clinical trials → FDA review → Approval → Postmarket surveillance.
items.back: Discovery → Preclinical testing → Clinical trials → FDA review → Approval → Postmarket surveillance.
items.cloze: From discovery to patient: {{c1::Discovery → Preclinical testing → Clinical trials → FDA review → Approval → Postmarket surveillance}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Most candidate drugs fail somewhere along this pipeline — approval is the exception, not the rule.
items.front: Most candidate drugs fail somewhere along this pipeline …
items.back: approval is the exception, not the rule.
items.cloze: Most candidate drugs fail somewhere along this pipeline … {{c1::approval is the exception, not the rule}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase I: safety, tolerability, dose-finding — a small group of healthy volunteers.
items.back: safety, tolerability, dose-finding — a small group of healthy volunteers.
items.cloze: Phase I: {{c1::safety, tolerability, dose-finding — a small group of healthy volunteers}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase II: preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile — a few hundred patients with the target condition.
items.back: preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile — a few hundred patients with the target condition.
items.cloze: Phase II: {{c1::preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile — a few hundred patients with the target condition}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase III: confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients, often multi-site.
items.back: confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients, often multi-site.
items.cloze: Phase III: {{c1::confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients, often multi-site}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase IV: postmarketing surveillance after approval — the general prescribed population.
items.back: postmarketing surveillance after approval — the general prescribed population.
items.cloze: Phase IV: {{c1::postmarketing surveillance after approval — the general prescribed population}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Every approved drug has passed through a structured development and regulatory pipeline (Phases I–IV).

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase II has the highest failure rate — only about 25% of new drugs move on to Phase III.
items.front: Phase II has the highest failure rate …
items.back: only about 25% of new drugs move on to Phase III.
items.cloze: Phase II has the {{c1::highest failure rate}} — only about 25% of new drugs move on to Phase III.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase III usually enrolls thousands of patients (Figure 1–6: 1000–6000), often double-blind and crossover, in settings like the drug's eventual use.
items.front: Phase III usually enrolls thousands of patients (Figure 1–6
items.back: 1000–6000), often double-blind and crossover, in settings like the drug's eventual use.
items.cloze: Phase III usually enrolls {{c1::thousands}} of patients (Figure 1–6: 1000–6000), often double-blind and crossover, in settings like the drug's eventual use.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Less than one-third of drugs studied in humans survive clinical trials and reach the market.

items.label: How it works
items.text: To see one case of a toxicity occurring 1 in 10,000, several hundred thousand patients may need exposure — so rare effects usually surface only in Phase IV, which has no fixed duration.
items.cloze: To see one case of a toxicity occurring 1 in 10,000, several hundred thousand patients may need exposure — so rare effects usually surface only in Phase IV, which has {{c1::no fixed duration}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Marketing requires a New Drug Application (NDA) after Phase III; human testing starts only after an IND (Investigational New Drug) application.
items.cloze: Marketing requires a {{c1::New Drug Application (NDA)}} after Phase III; human testing starts only after an {{c2::IND}} (Investigational New Drug) application.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Strength of evidence: case reports < cohort and case-control studies < randomized controlled trials (the gold standard: randomization balances confounders).
items.back: case reports < cohort and case-control studies < randomized controlled trials (the gold standard: randomization balances confounders).
items.cloze: Strength of evidence: case reports < cohort and case-control studies < {{c1::randomized controlled trials}} (the gold standard: randomization balances confounders).

items.label: Example
items.text: FDA MedWatch — an adverse-event reporting system.
items.cloze: FDA MedWatch — {{c1::an adverse-event reporting system}}.

items.label: Example
items.text: Biologic DMARDs (MSK unit, later) are a direct example of the "biotechnology" drug source.

items.label: Example
items.text: Thalidomide (sold in Europe as a "nontoxic" hypnotic) caused about 10,000 birth defects and led to the Kefauver-Harris Amendments (1962), which required proof of efficacy as well as safety.
items.cloze: {{c1::Thalidomide}} (sold in Europe as a "nontoxic" hypnotic) caused about 10,000 birth defects and led to the {{c2::Kefauver-Harris Amendments (1962)}}, which required proof of efficacy as well as safety.

items.label: Example
items.text: The Orphan Drug Amendment (1983) gives incentives for drugs treating diseases with fewer than 200,000 US patients.
items.cloze: The {{c1::Orphan Drug Amendment (1983)}} gives incentives for drugs treating diseases with fewer than 200,000 US patients.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why are rare adverse effects found after approval? Trials are too small and too short to catch 1-in-10,000 events — so they show up in Phase IV, in the general prescribed population.
items.front: Why are rare adverse effects found after approval?
items.back: Trials are too small and too short to catch 1-in-10,000 events — so they show up in Phase IV, in the general prescribed population.

items.text: Phases by question: I = Is it safe (healthy volunteers)? II = Is there an effect? III = Is it confirmed at scale? IV = Is it still safe in everyone?

items.label: Definition
items.text: Drug target: the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.
items.back: the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.
items.cloze: {{c1::Drug target}}: the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Receptor: a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.
items.back: a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.
items.cloze: {{c1::Receptor}}: a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Signal transduction: the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.
items.back: the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.
items.cloze: {{c1::Signal transduction}}: the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Pharmacologic response: the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.
items.back: the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.
items.cloze: {{c1::Pharmacologic response}}: the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Full agonist — maximal receptor activation.
items.cloze: Full agonist — {{c1::maximal receptor activation}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Partial agonist — submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.
items.back: submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.
items.cloze: Partial agonist — {{c1::submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Inverse agonist — reduces baseline (constitutive) receptor activity.
items.cloze: Inverse agonist — {{c1::reduces baseline (constitutive) receptor activity}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Competitive antagonist — reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist.
items.back: reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist.
items.cloze: Competitive antagonist — {{c1::reversibly competes with agonist at the same site}}; overcome by more agonist.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Noncompetitive antagonist — binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect.
items.back: binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect.
items.cloze: Noncompetitive antagonist — {{c1::binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Irreversible antagonist — permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.
items.back: permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.
items.cloze: Irreversible antagonist — {{c1::permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Kd: the drug concentration that fills half the receptors; a low Kd means high affinity.
items.back: the drug concentration that fills half the receptors; a low Kd means high affinity.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Albuterol is a selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist.
items.cloze: {{c1::Albuterol}} is a selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Binding activates the β2 receptor → increases intracellular cAMP.
items.cloze: Binding activates the β2 receptor … {{c1::increases intracellular cAMP}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Rising cAMP relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation.
items.front: Rising cAMP relaxes bronchial smooth muscle …
items.cloze: Rising cAMP relaxes bronchial smooth muscle … {{c1::bronchodilation}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: This is the same receptor-to-response logic you will reuse for every agonist drug this term.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Albuterol bridges introductory pharmacodynamics into the pulmonary pharmacology seen later in the curriculum.
items.cloze: {{c1::Albuterol}} bridges introductory pharmacodynamics into the pulmonary pharmacology seen later in the curriculum.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Competitive antagonism is surmountable in real life: exercise or stress raises catecholamines enough to overcome a fixed propranolol dose.
items.front: Competitive antagonism is surmountable in real life
items.back: exercise or stress raises catecholamines enough to overcome a fixed propranolol dose.
items.cloze: Competitive antagonism is surmountable in real life: {{c1::exercise or stress raises catecholamines enough to overcome a fixed propranolol dose}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Propranolol markedly slows the heart rate in pheochromocytoma (high catecholamines) but not the resting rate of a trained marathon runner.
items.cloze: {{c1::Propranolol}} markedly slows the heart rate in pheochromocytoma (high catecholamines) but not the resting rate of a trained marathon runner.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Glucocorticoids will not stop an acute asthma attack within minutes: gene-acting drugs need hours to make new proteins.
items.front: Glucocorticoids will not stop an acute asthma attack within minutes
items.back: gene-acting drugs need hours to make new proteins.
items.cloze: Glucocorticoids will not stop an acute asthma attack within minutes: {{c1::gene-acting drugs need hours to make new proteins}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors prolong second messengers: milrinone (cAMP) and sildenafil (cGMP).
items.cloze: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors prolong second messengers: {{c1::milrinone (cAMP) and sildenafil (cGMP)}}.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve right (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist lowers the Emax instead.
items.back: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve right (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist lowers the Emax instead.
items.cloze: Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve {{c1::right}} (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist {{c2::lowers the Emax}} instead.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism — potency falls, but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present.
items.back: only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present.
items.cloze: Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: {{c1::only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present}}.

items.text: Most drugs target receptors or enzymes — ion channels and transporters matter especially for cardiac and CNS drugs.

items.label: How it works
items.text: An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal; a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Spare receptors: a maximal response can occur without occupying every receptor (e.g., about 90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response still preserved).
items.back: a maximal response can occur without occupying every receptor (e.g., about 90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response still preserved).
items.cloze: {{c1::Spare receptors}}: a maximal response can occur without occupying every receptor (e.g., about 90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response still preserved).

items.label: How it works
items.text: Irreversible antagonist effects last until new receptors are made — duration depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination (phenoxybenzamine for pheochromocytoma).
items.front: Irreversible antagonist effects last until new receptors are made …
items.back: duration depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination (phenoxybenzamine for pheochromocytoma).
items.cloze: {{c1::Irreversible antagonist}} effects last until new receptors are made — duration depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination (phenoxybenzamine for pheochromocytoma).

items.label: How it works
items.text: A partial agonist's lower maximal effect is not due to lower affinity — it can occupy all receptors and still produce less response.
items.front: A partial agonist's lower maximal effect is not due to lower affinity …
items.back: it can occupy all receptors and still produce less response.
items.cloze: A partial agonist's lower maximal effect is {{c1::not}} due to lower affinity — it can occupy all receptors and still produce less response.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Allosteric modulators bind a different site from the agonist (e.g., benzodiazepines enhance GABA's effect).
items.cloze: {{c1::Allosteric modulators}} bind a different site from the agonist (e.g., benzodiazepines enhance GABA's effect).

items.label: How it works
items.text: Agonist-induced desensitization (tachyphylaxis) and downregulation reduce response with continued exposure.
items.cloze: Agonist-induced {{c1::desensitization}} (tachyphylaxis) and downregulation reduce response with continued exposure.

items.text: Targets beyond receptors: enzymes (statins on HMG-CoA reductase), transporters (digitalis on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; antidepressants) and structural proteins (colchicine on tubulin).

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why can more agonist overcome a competitive antagonist? Both compete reversibly for the same site — flood the site with agonist and it wins, so the curve shifts right but the same Emax is still reached.
items.front: Why can more agonist overcome a competitive antagonist?
items.back: Both compete reversibly for the same site — flood the site with agonist and it wins, so the curve shifts right but the same Emax is still reached.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why does albuterol open the airways? β2 activation → ↑ intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxes → bronchodilation.

items.back: β2 activation → ↑ intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxes → bronchodilation.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Potency: how much drug is required to produce a given effect — a more potent drug needs a lower dose.
items.back: how much drug is required to produce a given effect — a more potent drug needs a lower dose.
items.cloze: {{c1::Potency}}: how much drug is required to produce a given effect — a more potent drug needs a lower dose.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Efficacy (Emax): the maximum effect a drug can produce, no matter how high the dose goes.
items.back: the maximum effect a drug can produce, no matter how high the dose goes.
items.cloze: {{c1::Efficacy (Emax)}}: the maximum effect a drug can produce, no matter how high the dose goes.

items.label: Definition
items.text: EC₅₀: the drug concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.
items.back: the drug concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.
items.cloze: {{c1::EC₅₀}}: the drug concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).
items.back: TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).
items.cloze: Therapeutic Index (TI) = {{c1::TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%)}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Quantal dose-response: ED₅₀ (effective in 50%), TD₅₀ (toxic in 50%), LD₅₀ (lethal in 50% of animals).
items.back: ED₅₀ (effective in 50%), TD₅₀ (toxic in 50%), LD₅₀ (lethal in 50% of animals).
items.cloze: {{c1::Quantal dose-response}}: ED₅₀ (effective in 50%), TD₅₀ (toxic in 50%), LD₅₀ (lethal in 50% of animals).

items.label: Definition
items.text: Therapeutic window: the range between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — more practical than TI for dosing a patient.
items.back: the range between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — more practical than TI for dosing a patient.
items.cloze: {{c1::Therapeutic window}}: the range between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — more practical than TI for dosing a patient.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Potency clinically matters for dosing — not for choosing the "better" drug.
items.cloze: Potency clinically matters for dosing … {{c1::not for choosing the "better" drug}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.
items.front: Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency …
items.back: a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.
items.cloze: Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency … {{c1::a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: With a narrow TI, a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic — which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Students should be able to name all four narrow-TI drugs without hesitation and know that each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: No drug causes only a single specific effect — drugs are selective, not specific.
items.front: No drug causes only a single specific effect …
items.cloze: No drug causes only a single specific effect — drugs are {{c1::selective}}, not specific.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Asthma + hypertension on propranolol: nonselective β blockade can cause bronchoconstriction; a β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol) is an alternative.
items.back: nonselective β blockade can cause bronchoconstriction; a β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol) is an alternative.
items.cloze: Asthma + hypertension on propranolol: {{c1::nonselective β blockade can cause bronchoconstriction}}; a β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol) is an alternative.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: A drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy — potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."
items.front: A drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy …
items.back: potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Same Emax + lower dose needed = MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."
items.back: MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."
items.cloze: Same Emax + lower dose needed = {{c1::MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."}}

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: EC₅₀ measures potency — not toxicity and not bioavailability.
items.cloze: EC₅₀ measures potency — {{c1::not toxicity and not bioavailability}}.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: A narrow-TI drug is not "safer because it needs a lower dose" — it has a smaller margin and needs closer monitoring.
items.front: A narrow-TI drug is not "safer because it needs a lower dose" …
items.back: it has a smaller margin and needs closer monitoring.

items.label: How it works
items.text: The sigmoidal dose-response curve: x-axis = log(dose), y-axis = effect. EC₅₀ is on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau — the ceiling effect.
items.back: x-axis = log(dose), y-axis = effect. EC₅₀ is on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau — the ceiling effect.
items.cloze: The sigmoidal dose-response curve: {{c1::x-axis = log(dose), y-axis = effect}}. EC₅₀ is on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau — {{c2::the ceiling effect}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: EC₅₀ is read off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Lower EC₅₀ = more potent. Higher Emax = more efficacious.
items.back: more potent. Higher Emax = more efficacious.
items.cloze: Lower EC₅₀ = {{c1::more potent}}. Higher Emax = {{c2::more efficacious}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Potency and efficacy are independent properties — a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.
items.front: Potency and efficacy are independent properties …
items.back: a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.
items.cloze: Potency and efficacy are independent properties … {{c1::a drug can differ in one without differing in the other}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: A curve farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose (greater potency); curves reaching the same plateau height have identical Emax (efficacy).

items.label: How it works
items.text: A wide TI means a large margin between an effective dose and a toxic dose — generally safer to dose.

items.label: How it works
items.text: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.
items.front: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together …
items.back: requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.
items.cloze: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together … {{c1::requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers is the therapeutic index itself.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Dose-response curves describe potency and efficacy.

items.text: Classic narrow-TI drugs: warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why do narrow-TI drugs need blood levels? The effective dose and the toxic dose sit so close together that a small dosing error can push the patient from effective to toxic.
items.front: Why do narrow-TI drugs need blood levels?
items.back: The effective dose and the toxic dose sit so close together that a small dosing error can push the patient from effective to toxic.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why does efficacy beat potency clinically? Potency only changes the dose you give; efficacy sets the ceiling of what the drug can achieve at any dose.
items.front: Why does efficacy beat potency clinically?
items.back: Potency only changes the dose you give; efficacy sets the ceiling of what the drug can achieve at any dose.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Narrow-TI drugs — "Watch Levels During Prescribing": Warfarin, Lithium, Digoxin, Phenytoin.

items.text: TI = Toxic over Effective → TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic on top).

items.label: Definition
items.text: A — Absorption: movement of drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream.
items.back: movement of drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream.
items.cloze: A — Absorption: {{c1::movement of drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: D — Distribution: movement of drug from blood into tissues.
items.back: movement of drug from blood into tissues.
items.cloze: D — Distribution: {{c1::movement of drug from blood into tissues}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: M — Metabolism: chemical transformation of drug, mainly in the liver.
items.back: chemical transformation of drug, mainly in the liver.
items.cloze: M — Metabolism: {{c1::chemical transformation of drug, mainly in the liver}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: E — Excretion: removal of drug/metabolites from the body, mainly via the kidney.
items.back: removal of drug/metabolites from the body, mainly via the kidney.
items.cloze: E — Excretion: {{c1::removal of drug/metabolites from the body, mainly via the kidney}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.
items.back: the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.
items.cloze: Bioavailability (F) = {{c1::the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: First-pass effect: the liver metabolizes (can inactivate a large fraction of) an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.
items.back: the liver metabolizes (can inactivate a large fraction of) an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Volume of distribution (Vd): a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.
items.back: a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.
items.cloze: {{c1::Volume of distribution (Vd)}}: a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.

items.label: Definition
items.text: pKa: the pH at which a drug is half ionized and half nonionized.
items.back: the pH at which a drug is half ionized and half nonionized.
items.cloze: {{c1::pKa}}: the pH at which a drug is half ionized and half nonionized.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Routes that bypass first-pass metabolism: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.
items.back: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.
items.cloze: Routes that bypass first-pass metabolism: {{c1::essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism; oral dosing passes through the liver first.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Because the liver can inactivate a large fraction of drug first, some drugs are given sublingually or transdermally instead of orally.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.
items.front: A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well …
items.back: unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.
items.cloze: A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well … {{c1::unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Aspirin overdose: sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes blood and urine, reducing aspirin entry into tissues and speeding its renal excretion.
items.back: sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes blood and urine, reducing aspirin entry into tissues and speeding its renal excretion.
items.cloze: {{c1::Aspirin}} overdose: sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes blood and urine, reducing aspirin entry into tissues and speeding its renal excretion.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: IV = 100% bioavailable with no absorption phase; oral is less than 100%.
items.back: 100% bioavailable with no absorption phase; oral is less than 100%.
items.cloze: IV = {{c1::100% bioavailable with no absorption phase}}; oral is less than 100%.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Taking an oral drug with food or on an empty stomach does not bypass first-pass metabolism — sublingual does.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: A very high Vd does not mean a big anatomic space — it means the drug is mostly in tissue, not plasma.

items.back: it means the drug is mostly in tissue, not plasma.

items.text: ADME determines how much drug reaches its target and for how long.

items.text: Metabolism (M arrow → liver) and Excretion (E arrow → kidney) are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug; Absorption and Distribution govern how the drug arrives and spreads.

items.label: How it works
items.text: First-pass route: oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.
items.back: oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.
items.cloze: First-pass route: {{c1::oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly (no absorption step).
items.front: By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability …
items.back: the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly (no absorption step).
items.cloze: By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability … {{c1::the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly (no absorption step)}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Plasma protein binding: only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.
items.back: only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.
items.cloze: {{c1::Plasma protein binding}}: only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Lipid solubility: lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.
items.back: lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.
items.cloze: {{c1::Lipid solubility}}: lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Tissue perfusion: highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).
items.back: highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).
items.cloze: {{c1::Tissue perfusion}}: highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).

items.label: How it works
items.text: Vd is a theoretical volume, not a real anatomic space.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Blood-brain barrier — Why can some drugs readily enter the CNS while others cannot? Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement.
items.back: Why can some drugs readily enter the CNS while others cannot? Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement.
items.cloze: Blood-brain barrier — {{c1::Why can some drugs readily enter the CNS while others cannot?}} Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross the BBB more easily than large, polar, or highly protein-bound drugs.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Efflux transporters (like P-glycoprotein) can actively pump some drugs back out of the CNS.

items.label: How it works
items.text: First-pass loss can happen in the gut wall (e.g., intestinal CYP3A4) as well as the liver; grapefruit juice inhibits gut-wall metabolism and P-glycoprotein, raising absorption of some drugs.
items.cloze: First-pass loss can happen in the {{c1::gut wall}} (e.g., intestinal CYP3A4) as well as the liver; grapefruit juice inhibits gut-wall metabolism and P-glycoprotein, raising absorption of some drugs.

items.label: How it works
items.text: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) pumps drugs out of cells in brain, testes, and gut; inhibiting it raises digoxin blood levels.
items.cloze: {{c1::P-glycoprotein (MDR1)}} pumps drugs out of cells in brain, testes, and gut; inhibiting it raises digoxin blood levels.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Ion trapping: weak acids are excreted faster in alkaline urine; weak bases faster in acidic urine.
items.back: weak acids are excreted faster in alkaline urine; weak bases faster in acidic urine.
items.cloze: {{c1::Ion trapping}}: weak acids are excreted faster in {{c2::alkaline}} urine; weak bases faster in {{c3::acidic}} urine.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Drugs cross membranes by lipid diffusion (the main route), aqueous pores, carriers (saturable) or endocytosis (vitamin B₁₂, iron).
items.cloze: Drugs cross membranes by {{c1::lipid diffusion}} (the main route), aqueous pores, {{c2::carriers}} (saturable) or endocytosis (vitamin B₁₂, iron).

items.label: How it works
