items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient says they take no medications, but separately mentions using "Tylenol" for headaches and a combination cold-and-flu product. What does this scenario illustrate?

options.A: Brand names can obscure a shared generic ingredient, risking unintentional double-dosing
options.B: Chemical names are standardized internationally, so this mix-up could not happen
options.C: Generic names vary by manufacturer, which caused the confusion
options.D: Pharmacologic effect and therapeutic effect are simply two words for the same thing

items.why: Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient. Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In which clinical trial phase is a drug first tested in a large patient population specifically to confirm efficacy and monitor for adverse effects at scale, just before approval?

options.A: Phase I
options.B: Phase II
options.C: Phase III
options.D: Phase IV

items.why: Phase III trials enroll hundreds to thousands of patients, often at multiple sites, to confirm efficacy and monitor safety at scale before approval. Phase I is small-scale safety/dosing, Phase II is preliminary efficacy, and Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 1 above, the dashed curve (+ Competitive antagonist) is shifted to the right of the agonist-alone curve but reaches the same plateau at the top. What does this pattern show?

options.A: More agonist is needed to reach the same effect, but the same maximal effect is still achievable
options.B: The competitive antagonist lowers the drug’s efficacy (Emax)
options.C: The competitive antagonist increases the drug’s potency
options.D: The competitive antagonist has no measurable effect on the agonist’s curve

items.why: A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism: it takes more drug to reach a given effect (potency falls), but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax. Contrast this with the noncompetitive/irreversible curve in the same figure, which plateaus lower instead of shifting right.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A drug binds the same receptor as an endogenous agonist and lowers the tissue’s baseline (constitutive) activity below normal, without any agonist present. This drug is best classified as a(n):

options.A: Full agonist
options.B: Partial agonist
options.C: Competitive antagonist
options.D: Inverse agonist

items.why: An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal — a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: On the dose-response curve in Figure 2, the point marked EC₅₀ sits exactly halfway up the rising part of the curve. What does this point represent?

options.A: The dose at which the drug becomes toxic
options.B: The concentration producing 50% of the drug’s maximal effect
options.C: The point where the drug has zero effect
options.D: The drug’s bioavailability

items.why: EC₅₀ is read directly off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax (the plateau) — it is the standard graphical measure of potency, not a measure of toxicity or bioavailability.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In the left panel of Figure 3, Drug A’s curve sits to the left of Drug B’s curve, but both curves plateau at the same height. What does this tell you?

options.A: Drug A is more potent than Drug B, and both have equal efficacy
options.B: Drug A is more efficacious than Drug B
options.C: Drug A and Drug B have different Emax values
options.D: Drug B is more potent than Drug A

items.why: A curve positioned farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose — that is greater potency. Because both curves reach the same plateau height, their Emax (efficacy) is identical; only potency differs, exactly as the right panel then shows the reverse case (same potency, different efficacy).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Comparing the two number lines in Figure 4, the narrow-TI drug’s ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers sit much closer together than the wide-TI drug’s. What is the clinical implication?

options.A: The narrow-TI drug is safer because it requires a lower dose
options.B: The narrow-TI drug has a smaller margin between an effective and a toxic dose, requiring closer monitoring
options.C: The wide-TI drug is more likely to cause toxicity
options.D: Therapeutic index has no bearing on dosing safety

items.why: The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers on the number line is the therapeutic index itself — a narrow gap (as with warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin) means a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic, which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Drug X requires a much lower dose than Drug Y to achieve the same effect, but both drugs achieve the same maximum effect (Emax). Which statement is correct?

options.A: Drug X is more efficacious than Drug Y
options.B: Drug X is more potent than Drug Y
options.C: Drug X has a narrower therapeutic index than Drug Y
options.D: Drug X and Drug Y have different Emax values

items.why: Needing a lower dose for the same effect is the definition of greater potency. Since both drugs reach the same Emax, their efficacy is equal — potency and efficacy are independent properties.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 5, two separate arrows leave the Central Compartment box: one labeled "M" pointing to Metabolism (Liver), and one labeled "E" pointing to Excretion (Kidney). Together, these two arrows represent which part of ADME?

options.A: Absorption and Distribution
options.B: Distribution only
options.C: Metabolism and Excretion — how the drug is transformed and cleared
options.D: Only the Excretion step

items.why: The diagram shows drug leaving the Central Compartment by two separate routes: the "M" arrow to the liver (biotransformation) and the "E" arrow to the kidney (elimination). Together these are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug, as opposed to Absorption and Distribution, which govern how the drug arrives and spreads.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which route of administration bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism entirely, by entering systemic venous circulation directly?

options.A: Sublingual
options.B: Oral, taken on an empty stomach
options.C: All routes undergo first-pass metabolism equally
options.D: Oral, taken with food

items.why: Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver’s first-pass metabolism — unlike oral dosing, which is absorbed into the portal circulation and passes through the liver first.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 45-year-old patient takes a new medication exactly as prescribed. Drug levels are within the therapeutic range, yet the patient develops an unintended, harmful response. Which term best describes this event?

options.A: Toxicity, because any harmful drug response counts as toxicity
options.B: An adverse drug reaction, because it occurred at a normal therapeutic dose
options.C: A therapeutic effect, because the drug was taken exactly as prescribed
options.D: A pharmacologic effect only, because it was a measurable biological change
options.E: Irreversible antagonism, because the receptor was permanently inactivated

items.why: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses (S5).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes pharmacokinetics from pharmacodynamics?

options.A: Pharmacokinetics studies receptor binding; pharmacodynamics studies absorption and excretion
options.B: Pharmacokinetics applies only to IV drugs; pharmacodynamics applies only to oral drugs
options.C: Pharmacokinetics studies genetic variation; pharmacodynamics studies poisoning and overdose
options.D: Pharmacokinetics is what the drug does to the body; pharmacodynamics is what the body does to the drug
options.E: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body

items.why: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect) (S6).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A drug relieved symptoms in most participants of a controlled multi-site trial. In your clinic, far fewer patients improve; many miss doses and have several comorbidities. Which concept best explains the gap?

options.A: A narrow therapeutic index that appeared after approval
options.B: Lower potency than was measured during trial dose-finding
options.C: Extensive first-pass metabolism in the clinic's patients
options.D: Competitive antagonism of the drug by the comorbid conditions
options.E: Real-world effectiveness falling below the drug's trial efficacy

items.why: Efficacy is performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness is performance in everyday practice with real-world adherence and comorbidities (S14).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Two years after approval, reports reveal a serious reaction occurring in about 1 in 10,000 patients — never seen in the clinical trials. Which best explains why it was missed before approval?

options.A: Adverse-event reporting systems accept only voluntary reports
options.B: Approval came before the drug completed any clinical trial phase
options.C: Phase I trials enrolled patients who already had the target condition
options.D: Trial populations were too small and too short to detect so rare an event
options.E: Phase III trials are not designed to monitor adverse effects

items.why: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events (S12 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: According to the textbook, which clinical trial phase has the highest rate of drug failures?

options.A: Phase II
options.B: Phase IV
options.C: FDA review
options.D: Phase III
options.E: Phase I

items.why: Phase II has the highest failure rate; only about 25% of drugs move on to Phase III (p. 17).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 22-year-old patient inhales albuterol, and within minutes the bronchial smooth muscle relaxes. Which sequence best explains this effect?

options.A: β2 receptor blockade → falling intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.B: Enzyme inhibition → falling intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle dilation
options.C: β2 receptor activation → rising intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.D: Ion channel opening → rising intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle contraction
options.E: Inverse agonism at β2 → lowered baseline activity → smooth muscle relaxation

items.why: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: binding activates β2 → increases cAMP → relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation (S26).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient receives a drug that blocks a receptor. Raising the dose of the agonist medication eventually restores the full original maximal response. The blocking drug is most likely a(n):

options.A: Noncompetitive antagonist
options.B: Inverse agonist
options.C: Irreversible antagonist
options.D: Competitive antagonist
options.E: Partial agonist

items.why: A competitive antagonist reversibly competes at the same site and is overcome by more agonist — same Emax, curve shifted right (S22, S22 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 54-year-old is given phenoxybenzamine before surgery for pheochromocytoma. Blood pressure stays controlled even when the tumor releases large catecholamine surges. What best explains why the blockade persists?

options.A: It activates opposing receptors, producing a physiologic counter-effect instead
options.B: It binds receptors irreversibly; effect lasts until new receptors are made
options.C: It is a partial agonist that caps the maximal catecholamine response
options.D: It neutralizes catecholamines chemically in plasma before they reach receptors
options.E: It competes reversibly, so high catecholamine levels easily displace it

items.why: An irreversible antagonist's duration depends on receptor turnover, and high agonist levels cannot overcome it (p. 25).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient asks why an inhaled bronchodilator works in minutes but an oral corticosteroid takes hours. What best explains the corticosteroid’s delay?

options.A: It acts on an intracellular receptor that changes gene transcription
options.B: It is a partial agonist with low efficacy
options.C: It acts on a ligand-gated ion channel
options.D: It must first be activated by CYP2D6
options.E: It binds a G protein–coupled receptor that raises cAMP

items.why: Gene-acting drugs need time to make new proteins, so effects lag 30 minutes to several hours (p. 28).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A drug activates a receptor coupled to Gq. Which change follows inside the cell?

options.A: Adenylyl cyclase is stimulated, so cAMP rises
options.B: Phospholipase C makes IP₃ and DAG; calcium rises
options.C: Phosphodiesterase breaks down cGMP in the cell
options.D: A JAK kinase activates STAT transcription proteins
options.E: Adenylyl cyclase is inhibited, so cAMP falls

items.why: Gq stimulates phospholipase C, producing IP₃ (calcium release) and DAG (protein kinase C) (p. 32; p. 35).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A PA is starting a patient on lithium. Compared with a drug that has a wide therapeutic index, what does lithium's narrow therapeutic index mean for this patient's care?

options.A: Lithium is more potent, so it can be dosed without monitoring levels
options.B: Lithium has a higher Emax, so lower doses than usual are always enough
options.C: Lithium is 100% bioavailable, so blood levels never need to be checked
options.D: Effective and toxic doses are close, so dose carefully and monitor blood levels
options.E: Lithium has a large safety margin, so dosing errors are well tolerated

items.why: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requiring careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring; lithium is a classic narrow-TI drug (S38).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Two drugs relieve the same symptom. Drug A works at 5 mg and Drug B at 50 mg, but at maximal doses Drug B produces a much greater maximal effect. Which statement best guides drug selection?

options.A: Drug B has greater efficacy, which matters more clinically than Drug A's potency
options.B: Drug A should be chosen because greater potency means it works better
options.C: Both drugs have equal efficacy because both relieve the same symptom
options.D: Drug A has greater efficacy because it needs a much smaller dose
options.E: Drug B has greater potency because its maximal effect is much higher

items.why: Efficacy (Emax) clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless (S34).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient stable on IV propranolol is switched to the oral form and needs a much higher oral dose to reach the same systemic exposure. Which best explains this?

options.A: Propranolol has a narrow therapeutic index, so oral doses must be higher
options.B: Extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism lowers the drug's oral bioavailability
options.C: Propranolol is highly protein-bound, so the oral form is inactive in plasma
options.D: The IV form was less than 100% bioavailable, so less drug reached the blood
options.E: Oral propranolol cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so more must be given

items.why: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect; oral doses pass GI → portal → liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV exposure (S51, S50).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with meningitis receives a highly polar antibiotic. Which statement best describes this drug's ability to reach the CNS?

options.A: Polar drugs never reach the CNS, even when the meninges are inflamed
options.B: Polar drugs cross easily because P-glycoprotein pumps them into the CNS
options.C: Polar drugs usually cross poorly, but inflamed meninges allow better entry
options.D: Polar drugs cross easily because tight junctions favor polar molecules
options.E: Polar drugs cross well because the brain is a poorly perfused tissue

items.why: A highly polar antibiotic generally would not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis (S53 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient overdoses on a weak-acid drug. To speed its renal excretion, what should be done to the urine?

options.A: Make the urine more acidic
options.B: Slow glomerular filtration
options.C: Keep urine pH unchanged and give more fluids only
options.D: Raise plasma protein binding
options.E: Make the urine more alkaline

items.why: In alkaline urine a weak acid is mostly ionized, so it cannot diffuse back across the tubule and is trapped in the urine (p. 10).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A hospitalized patient receives a drug intravenously. Why is the bioavailability of this dose 100%?

options.A: The whole dose enters the bloodstream directly
options.B: IV drugs are always more potent than oral
options.C: IV drugs avoid all protein binding in plasma
options.D: IV drugs have the longest half-lives of all
options.E: IV drugs are never metabolized by the liver

items.why: IV has 100% bioavailability by definition — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly; there is no absorption step.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient's drug has a very high calculated volume of distribution (Vd). What does this suggest?

options.A: Rapid renal clearance of the drug
options.B: A large real anatomic space for the drug
options.C: High oral bioavailability of the drug
options.D: Most of the drug remains in plasma
options.E: Extensive distribution of drug into tissues

items.why: Vd relates total drug in the body to plasma concentration; a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: On number lines, a narrow-TI drug's ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ sit close together. What is the implication?

options.A: The wide-TI drug is more likely toxic
options.B: A small error can move effective to toxic
options.C: TI has no real bearing on dosing safety
options.D: The drug must have a lower Emax overall
options.E: The drug is safer because it needs less

items.why: The ED₅₀–TD₅₀ gap is the TI; a narrow gap means a small dosing error can push a patient from effective to toxic.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Years after approval, a drug's label gains a new warning based on reports clinicians submitted to FDA MedWatch. What is MedWatch?

options.A: An FDA drug-repurposing program
options.B: An FDA adverse-event reporting system
options.C: An FDA Phase III trial registry
options.D: An FDA dose-finding Phase I program
options.E: An FDA generic-name database

items.why: Adverse-event reporting: ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient receives an IV drug. Which tissues will the drug reach most slowly?

options.A: Brain and heart
options.B: Brain and kidney
options.C: Heart and kidney
options.D: Fat and bone
options.E: Fat and heart

items.why: Highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which receptor subtypes are listed under the receptor target class?

options.A: G-protein-coupled, voltage-gated, enzyme-linked, nuclear
options.B: Plasma-protein, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear
options.C: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, DNA
options.D: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, transporter-linked, nuclear
options.E: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear

items.why: Receptors: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient needs a rapid local effect in the lungs while minimizing systemic exposure. Which route fits?

options.A: Intravenous (IV)
options.B: Inhaled
options.C: Topical
options.D: Transdermal
options.E: Intramuscular (IM)

items.why: Inhaled: rapid local effect in the lungs; minimizes systemic exposure for some drugs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A trial enrolls a few hundred patients with the target condition to estimate preliminary efficacy and side effects. Which phase is this?

options.A: Phase I
options.B: Phase II
options.C: Phase III
options.D: Phase IV
options.E: FDA review

items.why: Phase II = preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile in a few hundred patients with the target condition.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement about lipid solubility and distribution is correct?

options.A: Lipophilic drugs cannot enter fatty tissue
options.B: Lipophilic drugs stay mainly within plasma
options.C: Lipophilic drugs cross membranes and enter fat
options.D: Polar drugs cross membranes most readily
options.E: Lipid solubility has no effect on spread

items.why: Lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which two factors reduce oral bioavailability?

options.A: Incomplete absorption and renal excretion
options.B: High lipid solubility and tissue perfusion
options.C: Protein binding and first-pass metabolism
options.D: Incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism
options.E: First-pass metabolism and a high Vd

items.why: Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement about potency and efficacy is correct?

options.A: Higher potency always means higher efficacy
options.B: Efficacy is the dose needed for effect
options.C: A lower EC₅₀ means a lower potency
options.D: They are independent drug properties
options.E: Potency matters more than efficacy clinically

items.why: Potency and efficacy are independent properties — a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which target class directly gates the flow of ions across a membrane?

options.A: Enzymes
options.B: Ion channels
options.C: Nucleic acids
options.D: Nuclear receptors
options.E: Transporters

items.why: Ion channels directly gate the flow of ions across a membrane.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A PA counsels a patient who buys several brand-name and store-brand products. Why should the PA prescribe and counsel by generic name?

options.A: Generic names change between countries
options.B: Generic names are the marketed trade names
options.C: Generic names are unambiguous and international
options.D: Generic names describe the exact structure
options.E: Generic names differ for each manufacturer

items.why: Generic names are unambiguous and international, avoiding confusion when one ingredient hides under multiple brand names.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Monoclonal antibodies and gene- or cell-based therapies belong to which source of new drugs?

options.A: Biologics
options.B: Natural products
options.C: Drug repurposing
options.D: Postmarket surveillance
options.E: Synthetic small molecules

items.why: Biologics = monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drug did the lecture use as an example of a very high Vd?

options.A: Digoxin
options.B: Albuterol
options.C: Morphine
options.D: Lithium
options.E: Heparin

items.why: Digoxin has a very high Vd — it is mostly sequestered in tissue, not floating around in plasma.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which chain correctly orders the pharmacodynamic pathway?

options.A: Target → drug → response → signal transduction
options.B: Drug → target → signal transduction → response
options.C: Drug → response → target → signal transduction
options.D: Drug → absorption → excretion → response
options.E: Drug → signal transduction → target → response

items.why: Drug → target → signal transduction → response; every PD topic maps onto this chain.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: How is the therapeutic index calculated?

options.A: TD₅₀ divided by ED₅₀
options.B: Emax divided by ED₅₀
options.C: EC₅₀ divided by Emax
options.D: TD₅₀ minus ED₅₀
options.E: ED₅₀ divided by TD₅₀

items.why: Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which sequence describes the first-pass route of an oral drug?

options.A: GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic
options.B: GI tract → systemic → liver → portal circulation
options.C: GI tract → portal circulation → systemic → liver
options.D: GI tract → kidney → portal circulation → systemic
options.E: GI tract → liver → portal circulation → systemic

items.why: Oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement about pharmacologic and therapeutic effects is correct?

options.A: They are two words for the same thing
options.B: Every pharmacologic effect is intended
options.C: A therapeutic effect need not be measurable
options.D: Therapeutic effects occur only above range
options.E: A pharmacologic effect may not be therapeutic

items.why: A drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic — that is often exactly what an adverse effect is.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A PA wants a patient's drug to avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism. Which route enters systemic venous circulation directly?

options.A: Oral, taken together with food
options.B: Oral, as an extended-release form
options.C: Oral, as a crushed tablet
options.D: Sublingual, under-the-tongue absorption
options.E: Oral, taken on an empty stomach

items.why: Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which organs receive a drug fastest during distribution?

options.A: Bone, kidney, and fat
options.B: Fat, heart, and bone
options.C: Skin, fat, and liver
options.D: Fat, bone, and skin
options.E: Brain, heart, and kidney

items.why: Highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient inhales albuterol and the airways open within minutes. Which sequence explains this?

options.A: β2 blockade → ↓ cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.B: β2 activation → ↓ cAMP → smooth muscle contraction
options.C: β2 activation → ↑ cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.D: Enzyme inhibition → ↓ cAMP → bronchodilation
options.E: Ion channel opening → ↑ cAMP → contraction

items.why: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: β2 activation → increased intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxation → bronchodilation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L01 S34; S34 (notes); L02 S48; SG U1-R6
items.stem: Two drugs treat the same symptom. Drug A works at 5 mg; Drug B needs 50 mg but reaches a higher maximal effect. Which matters more for choice?

options.A: Neither, since both work
options.B: Drug A's greater efficacy
options.C: Drug B's greater efficacy
options.D: Drug A's greater potency
options.E: Drug B's greater potency

items.why: Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Two years after approval, a serious reaction appears in about 1 in 10,000 patients. Why was it missed earlier?

options.A: Approval occurs before any human trials
options.B: Phase III never monitors any adverse effects
options.C: Trials were too small and short to detect it
options.D: Phase I enrolled patients with the condition
options.E: Reporting systems accept only voluntary reports

items.why: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trials are too small and too short to catch 1-in-10,000 events.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24) starts a narrow-TI antiarrhythmic eliminated unchanged by the kidney; she began a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor 3 weeks ago. What is the FIRST concern?

options.A: Reduced renal clearance shortening the half-life
options.B: CYP3A4 induction lowering the antiarrhythmic level
options.C: Increased Vd from her advanced kidney disease
options.D: First-pass metabolism blocking oral absorption
options.E: Reduced renal clearance raising level and half-life

items.why: CKD reduces renal clearance, raising the drug's concentration and prolonging its half-life regardless of the new drug.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which name describes a drug's exact molecular structure?

options.A: The store-brand name
options.B: The chemical name
options.C: The brand name
options.D: The trade name
options.E: The generic name

items.why: The chemical name describes the exact molecular structure and is rarely used in clinical practice.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes a drug that is highly bound to plasma proteins. Which fraction of it is active and able to cross membranes?

options.A: The ionized, polar fraction
options.B: The unbound, free fraction
options.C: The protein-bound fraction
options.D: The conjugated Phase II fraction
options.E: The fraction stored in fat

items.why: Only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A PA starts lithium. Compared with a wide-TI drug, what does lithium's narrow TI mean for care?

options.A: Skip levels since IV is fully bioavailable
options.B: Skip monitoring since the margin is wide
options.C: Use lower doses since Emax is higher
options.D: Dose freely since potency is high
options.E: Dose carefully and monitor blood levels

items.why: Narrow TI: effective and toxic doses are close — careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A healthy 25-year-old volunteer joins a small study testing a new drug's safety, tolerability, and dosing. Which phase is this?

options.A: Phase III
options.B: Phase IV
options.C: Preclinical testing
options.D: Phase II
options.E: Phase I

items.why: Phase I = safety, tolerability, dose-finding in a small group of healthy volunteers.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drugs did the lecture name as having a large first-pass effect?

options.A: Nitroglycerin, warfarin, morphine
options.B: Nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine
options.C: Nitroglycerin, propranolol, albuterol
options.D: Digoxin, propranolol, morphine
options.E: Nitroglycerin, propranolol, lithium

items.why: Large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all need higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) for the same exposure as IV.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: For the same patient (stage 4 CKD, narrow-TI renally cleared antiarrhythmic, CYP3A4 inhibitor), what should happen before dispensing?

options.A: Check eGFR/CrCl, reduce dose or extend interval
options.B: Shorten the interval to reach steady state faster
options.C: Raise the dose to offset the CYP3A4 inhibitor
options.D: Stop all monitoring since the drug is oral
options.E: Give the standard dose and recheck labs in a year

items.why: Before dispensing: check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and monitor renal function and signs of toxicity closely after starting.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes twice the prescribed dose; serum levels rise above the therapeutic range and harm follows. What is this?

options.A: Enzyme induction
options.B: A therapeutic effect
options.C: An adverse drug reaction
options.D: Drug toxicity
options.E: An inverse agonist effect

items.why: Toxicity = harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient is prescribed an older, already-approved drug for a condition it was recently found to treat. Which source of new drugs is this?

options.A: Biologics
options.B: Synthetic and biotech
options.C: Postmarket surveillance
options.D: Natural products
options.E: Drug repurposing

items.why: Drug repurposing = an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Drug X needs a lower dose than Drug Y for the same effect; both reach the same Emax. Which is true?

options.A: X has the narrower therapeutic index
options.B: X is more potent and more efficacious
options.C: Y is more potent; efficacy is equal
options.D: X is more efficacious; potency is equal
options.E: X is more potent; efficacy is equal

items.why: Lower dose for the same effect = greater potency; same Emax = equal efficacy. Potency and efficacy are independent.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A critically ill patient needs immediate drug onset with no absorption phase. Which route fits?

options.A: Sublingual
options.B: Intramuscular (IM)
options.C: Subcutaneous (SC)
options.D: Transdermal
options.E: Intravenous (IV)

items.why: IV: 100% bioavailable, immediate onset, no absorption phase.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L01 S6; SG U1-R1; L02 S44
items.stem: Which statement correctly pairs each branch with its question?

options.A: PK: body acts on drug; PD: drug acts on body
options.B: PK: drug acts on body; PD: body acts on drug
options.C: PK: drug development stages; PD: postmarketing safety signals
options.D: PK: receptor binding and effect; PD: absorption and excretion
options.E: PK: genetic variation in response; PD: poisoning and overdose

items.why: Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME); pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which four drugs did the lecture name as classic narrow-therapeutic-index drugs?

options.A: Warfarin, lithium, morphine, phenytoin
options.B: Warfarin, albuterol, digoxin, phenytoin
options.C: Warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin
options.D: Heparin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin
options.E: Warfarin, lithium, digoxin, propranolol

items.why: Classic narrow-TI drugs: warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin — each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: According to the course study guide, which factor can ALSO lower real-world effectiveness below trial efficacy?

options.A: Strict adherence to the dosing schedule
options.B: Enrollment of healthy Phase I volunteers
options.C: Use of the IV route instead of oral
options.D: Drug interactions in everyday practice
options.E: Higher potency than the trial drug

items.why: The study guide adds that adherence, comorbidities, AND interactions can all reduce effectiveness below trial efficacy.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which antagonist permanently inactivates its receptor until new receptor is synthesized?

options.A: An irreversible antagonist
options.B: A competitive antagonist
options.C: A noncompetitive antagonist
options.D: An inverse agonist
options.E: A partial agonist

items.why: Irreversible antagonist = permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with meningitis receives a highly polar antibiotic. How does this drug reach the CNS?

options.A: Easily, since tight junctions favor polar drugs
options.B: Easily, since the brain is poorly perfused
options.C: Easily, since P-glycoprotein pumps it inward
options.D: Poorly normally, better with inflamed meninges
options.E: Never, even when the meninges are inflamed

items.why: A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient receives a drug that occupies every one of its receptors yet produces only a submaximal response. What is the drug?

options.A: A competitive antagonist
options.B: An inverse agonist
options.C: A full agonist
options.D: A partial agonist
options.E: An irreversible antagonist

items.why: Partial agonist = submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on a standard dose with levels inside the therapeutic range develops an unintended, harmful reaction. What is this?

options.A: Drug toxicity
options.B: A first-pass effect
options.C: Competitive antagonism
options.D: An adverse drug reaction
options.E: A therapeutic effect

items.why: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: If that antiarrhythmic were cleared mainly by hepatic CYP3A4 instead of the kidney, which concern would dominate?

options.A: A TPMT-related thiopurine toxicity
options.B: The direct renal clearance problem
options.C: The CYP3A4 inhibitor interaction
options.D: An HLA-linked hypersensitivity risk
options.E: Reduced first-pass oral bioavailability

items.why: If hepatically/CYP3A4 cleared, the renal concern is less central (CKD can still indirectly affect hepatic handling), and the CYP3A4 interaction becomes dominant.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: With no agonist present, a drug lowers a receptor's baseline activity below normal. What is it?

options.A: An inverse agonist
options.B: A noncompetitive antagonist
options.C: A full agonist
options.D: A partial agonist
options.E: A competitive antagonist

items.why: An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A PA needs a drug to reach a patient's central nervous system. Which drug properties favor crossing the blood-brain barrier?

options.A: Small, polar, and highly protein-bound
options.B: Small, ionized, and highly protein-bound
options.C: Small, lipophilic, and non-ionized
options.D: Large, lipophilic, and non-ionized
options.E: Large, polar, and highly protein-bound

items.why: Small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross the BBB more easily than large, polar, or highly protein-bound drugs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient is switched from an IV to an oral form of the same drug, and less of each dose now reaches the circulation. Which branch describes this change?

options.A: Pharmacokinetics, because it concerns absorption
options.B: Pharmacodynamics, because it concerns receptor binding
options.C: Pharmacogenomics, because it concerns genetic variation
options.D: Toxicology, because it concerns poisoning risk
options.E: Pharmacodynamics, because it concerns drug effect

items.why: Bioavailability is the fraction of a dose reaching systemic circulation — an absorption (ADME) property, so it is pharmacokinetics.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement about routes and first-pass metabolism matches the lecture?

options.A: All routes undergo first-pass equally
options.B: IM and SC undergo first-pass like oral
options.C: Essentially every route except oral bypasses it
options.D: Only the IV route bypasses first-pass
options.E: Transdermal is subject to first-pass

items.why: Routes that bypass first-pass: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: On a dose-response curve, what does EC₅₀ measure?

options.A: Toxicity — the dose harming 50% of patients
options.B: Potency — concentration giving 50% of Emax
options.C: Efficacy — the maximal effect possible
options.D: Safety — the gap between effect and harm
options.E: Bioavailability — fraction reaching circulation

items.why: EC₅₀ = the concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient will inject insulin at home. Which route did the lecture describe as slower, steady absorption, common for insulin and heparin?

options.A: Inhaled
options.B: Transdermal
options.C: Sublingual
options.D: Intramuscular (IM)
options.E: Subcutaneous (SC)

items.why: Subcutaneous (SC): slower, steady absorption; common for insulin, heparin.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which definition matches toxicity as taught in this unit?

options.A: Harm that occurs at normal therapeutic doses only
options.B: The intended, beneficial effect for a condition
options.C: Loss of effect after a CYP inducer is added
options.D: Any measurable biological change a drug produces
options.E: Harm as dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range

items.why: Toxicity = harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L01 S7; S7 (notes); S9; SG U1-R2
items.stem: A patient takes "Tylenol" for headaches and separately takes acetaminophen. What is the main risk?

options.A: A CYP3A4 interaction between two different drugs
options.B: No risk, since brand and generic names differ
options.C: Unintentional double-dosing of the same ingredient
options.D: Competitive antagonism at the same receptor site
options.E: Reduced bioavailability from first-pass metabolism

items.why: Tylenol is a brand of acetaminophen; taking both doubles the dose. Check for accidental double-dosing.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient stable on IV propranolol switches to oral and needs a much higher dose for the same exposure. Why?

options.A: Oral propranolol cannot cross the blood-brain barrier
options.B: High protein binding inactivates the oral form
options.C: Extensive first-pass metabolism lowers oral bioavailability
options.D: A narrow therapeutic index requires higher oral doses
options.E: The IV form was less than fully bioavailable

items.why: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect: oral doses pass the liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient's drug enters the brain poorly. Which BBB structure restricts paracellular movement?

options.A: Highly perfused capillaries of the brain
options.B: Tight junctions between endothelial cells
options.C: Plasma proteins binding the free drug
options.D: Lipid membranes favoring polar drugs
options.E: P-glycoprotein efflux pumps in the CNS

items.why: Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement at the blood-brain barrier.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What does P-glycoprotein do at the blood-brain barrier?

options.A: Pumps some drugs back out of the CNS
options.B: Binds free drug in the plasma permanently
options.C: Forms the tight junctions between cells
options.D: Pumps some drugs into the CNS actively
options.E: Metabolizes drugs within the brain tissue

items.why: Efflux transporters like P-glycoprotein can actively pump some drugs back out of the CNS.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A drug worked in most trial patients but helps fewer patients in clinic, where doses are missed and comorbidities are common. What explains this?

options.A: Phase III trials overestimated toxicity
options.B: The drug has a narrow therapeutic index
options.C: Potency is lower than trial potency
options.D: Effectiveness is lower than trial efficacy
options.E: Oral first-pass metabolism is higher

items.why: Efficacy = performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness = everyday practice with real adherence, comorbidities (and drug interactions).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which list gives the five major drug target classes?

options.A: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, lipids, nucleic acids
options.B: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, plasma proteins
options.C: Receptors, hormones, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids
options.D: Receptors, ion channels, antibodies, transporters, nucleic acids
options.E: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids

items.why: Five target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, and nucleic acids.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: On log-dose curves, Drug A sits left of Drug B, and both plateau at the same height. What does this show?

options.A: A and B have different Emax values
options.B: A is more efficacious; potency is identical
options.C: B is more potent; efficacy is identical
options.D: A is more potent; efficacy is identical
options.E: A has the wider therapeutic index

items.why: A curve farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose (greater potency); the same plateau height means identical Emax.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A drug relieves a chronic, non-life-threatening condition in 70% of patients but causes serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. How should a PA weigh it?

options.A: Compare it with the available alternatives
options.B: Use it only if Phase I showed no toxicity
options.C: Reject it, since any toxicity is unacceptable
options.D: Decide by its potency relative to others
options.E: Accept it, since 70% benefit outweighs any risk

items.why: Risk-benefit analysis is always comparative: a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if safer alternatives exist.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: In a 70-kg adult, Drug X has a Vd of 5 L and Drug Y has a Vd of 500 L. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Drug X is mostly in tissue, not plasma
options.B: Drug Y occupies a real 500-L body space
options.C: Vd shows which drug is more potent
options.D: Both drugs are mostly confined to plasma
options.E: Drug Y is mostly in tissue, not plasma

items.why: A high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution; it is a calculated, theoretical volume. Digoxin, with a Vd of about 500 L, is the classic example.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient received an irreversible antagonist; its plasma level is now undetectable, yet the blockade persists for days. Why?

options.A: Recovery must wait for new receptor synthesis
options.B: Protein binding keeps the drug active
options.C: Its plasma half-life is several days
options.D: Competitive binding still holds the site
options.E: The drug slowly leaks back out of fat

items.why: An irreversible antagonist permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized, so its effect depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on digoxin has nausea and a level of 2.6 ng/mL (textbook target about 1 ng/mL; toxic above 2). What is the best interpretation?

options.A: The level is in the toxic range for a narrow-TI drug
options.B: Digoxin levels are not clinically useful
options.C: Nausea proves the drug is ineffective
options.D: The level is ideal; continue the same dose
options.E: The level is low; increase the dose

items.why: Digoxin is a classic narrow-TI drug (target ~1 ng/mL, toxic >2 ng/mL in the textbook table); small changes push it into toxicity, so levels are monitored.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An older patient brings two bottles with different brand names; both list acetaminophen as the active ingredient. What is the best counseling step?

options.A: Assume the two brands are different drugs
options.B: Advise relabeling both by chemical name
options.C: Stop the store brand since brands differ
options.D: Name the shared generic and flag the duplicate
options.E: Reassure that OTC products are always safe

items.why: Counseling by generic name exposes a shared ingredient hidden under multiple brand names, preventing double-dosing.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A researcher studies why the same codeine dose relieves pain in one patient but not in their sibling, because of inherited enzyme differences. Which branch is this?

options.A: Pharmacodynamics alone
options.B: Pharmacogenomics
options.C: Pharmacokinetics alone
options.D: Toxicology
options.E: Drug development

items.why: Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation shapes an individual's drug response (e.g., CYP2D6 and codeine).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: How does protamine reverse heparin's anticoagulant effect?

options.A: It competes with heparin at its receptor
options.B: It irreversibly inactivates the receptor
options.C: It binds heparin directly (chemical antagonism)
options.D: It induces enzymes that clear heparin
options.E: It activates opposing receptors instead

items.why: Positively charged protamine binds negatively charged heparin, neutralizing it — chemical antagonism needs no receptor.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: On a quantal dose-response curve, what does ED₅₀ mean?

options.A: The dose that is toxic in 50% of subjects
options.B: The dose at which 50% of individuals respond
options.C: The dose that is lethal in 50% of animals
options.D: The dose giving 50% of one patient's Emax
options.E: The fraction of a dose that is absorbed

items.why: In quantal curves, ED₅₀ is the dose at which 50% of individuals show the specified effect (different from graded EC₅₀).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient needs slow, sustained systemic drug delivery through the skin over several days. Which route fits?

options.A: Sublingual
options.B: Inhaled
options.C: Transdermal
options.D: Topical
options.E: Intravenous

items.why: Transdermal: slow, sustained systemic absorption through the skin (and it avoids hepatic first-pass).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A second drug displaces a highly protein-bound drug from plasma proteins. What does the textbook say usually happens?

options.A: Free drug rises briefly, then returns to baseline
options.B: Total drug level always rises permanently
options.C: Bound drug becomes the active fraction
options.D: Free drug stays high for as long as both are given
options.E: Displacement always causes serious toxicity

items.why: If unbound drug rises from displacement, its elimination increases, and after about four half-lives the unbound concentration returns to its previous value (if unbound clearance is unchanged).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: After a brand's patent expires, how does a generic version usually win FDA approval?

options.A: Postmarketing MedWatch safety reports
options.B: An IND application for first human testing
options.C: A full new application with new Phase III trials
options.D: An abbreviated application with bioequivalence data
options.E: Orphan-drug designation for a rare disease

items.why: Generic manufacturers file an abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) showing bioequivalence; patents last 20 years.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Some antimicrobials and gene therapies act on which drug target class?

options.A: Ion channels
options.B: Nucleic acids (DNA/RNA)
options.C: Nuclear receptors
options.D: Transporters
options.E: Enzymes

items.why: Transporters & nucleic acids: carrier proteins; or DNA/RNA for some antimicrobials & gene therapies.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which law first required proof of efficacy, not just safety, for new drugs (after the thalidomide disaster)?

options.A: Orphan Drug Amendment (1983)
options.B: Durham-Humphrey Act (1952)
options.C: Kefauver-Harris Amendments (1962)
options.D: Drug Price Competition Act (1984)
options.E: Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (1938)

items.why: The Kefauver-Harris Amendments (1962) required proof of efficacy as well as safety; thalidomide's birth defects spurred them.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Paracelsus wrote that "the dose makes the poison." What does this mean?

options.A: Drugs become harmless at very high doses
options.B: Only true poisons can ever cause harm
options.C: Any substance can harm at the wrong dose
options.D: Harm depends mostly on the brand name
options.E: Toxins are always made in a laboratory

items.why: The textbook explains Paracelsus's point: any substance can be harmful if taken in the wrong dosage.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with angina is told to place nitroglycerin under the tongue rather than swallow it. Why?

options.A: Swallowed tablets cannot be absorbed at all
options.B: Swallowing it causes nitroglycerin toxicity
options.C: Sublingual dosing makes the drug more potent
options.D: Sublingual dosing lengthens its half-life
options.E: Sublingual dosing avoids its large first-pass loss

items.why: Nitroglycerin has a large first-pass effect; sublingual absorption enters systemic veins directly, bypassing the portal vein and liver.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Drug A has an EC₅₀ of 2 mg and reaches 60% of maximal response; Drug B has an EC₅₀ of 20 mg and reaches 100%. Which is true?

options.A: B is more potent; A is more efficacious
options.B: B is more potent and more efficacious
options.C: They are equal, since both relieve symptoms
options.D: A is more potent; B is more efficacious
options.E: A is more potent and more efficacious

items.why: Lower EC₅₀ = more potent (Drug A). Higher Emax = more efficacious (Drug B). Potency and efficacy are independent.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which term describes an inactive precursor that the body converts into the active drug?

options.A: A prodrug
options.B: A competitive antagonist
options.C: An active metabolite
options.D: A generic equivalent
options.E: A toxic metabolite

items.why: A prodrug is an inactive precursor converted to the active drug, usually by metabolism — one of the purposes of metabolism is to activate a prodrug.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An oral dose of 100 mg delivers 40 mg unchanged to the systemic circulation. What is its bioavailability (F)?
items.why: F = fraction of an administered dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged = 40 mg ÷ 100 mg = 40%.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on propranolol has a well-controlled resting heart rate, but during hard exercise the rate rises markedly. What best explains this?

options.A: Exercise induces CYP enzymes immediately
options.B: Propranolol acts as a full agonist in exercise
options.C: Propranolol is irreversible, so it wears off
options.D: Exercise permanently destroys β receptors
options.E: Surging catecholamines outcompete the blocker

items.why: With a competitive antagonist, the response depends on how much agonist competes: exercise-driven norepinephrine and epinephrine can overcome a fixed propranolol dose.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A drug's volume of distribution is about 0.04 L/kg (about 2.8 L in a 70-kg adult). Where is it mostly found?

options.A: In total body water
options.B: In extracellular water
options.C: In body fat
options.D: In the plasma
options.E: Sequestered in tissues

items.why: A drug restricted to the plasma has a Vd near the plasma volume, about 0.04 L/kg (2.8 L/70 kg); large protein molecules such as antibodies behave this way.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement reflects the textbook's view of drug selectivity?

options.A: Each drug binds only one receptor type
options.B: Side effects occur only at toxic doses
options.C: No drug causes only a single specific effect
options.D: Selectivity is the same as efficacy
options.E: Potent drugs are always more selective

items.why: Drugs are selective rather than specific: no drug causes only a single effect, so 'side effects' are expected pharmacologic effects.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A new cancer drug expected to be highly toxic enters its first human trial. According to the textbook, who is enrolled?

options.A: No humans, only animals, until approval
options.B: Healthy volunteers, as in usual Phase I
options.C: Thousands of patients at many sites
options.D: The general prescribed population
options.E: Volunteer patients who have the cancer

items.why: Phase I usually uses 20–100 healthy volunteers, but if significant toxicity is expected (e.g., cancer, AIDS), volunteer patients with the disease take part instead.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Before approval, a new drug is compared with standard care in 3,000 patients at 40 hospitals to confirm efficacy and watch for adverse effects. Which phase is this?

options.A: Phase III
options.B: Phase I
options.C: Preclinical
options.D: Phase IV
options.E: Phase II

items.why: Phase III confirms efficacy and monitors adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients (textbook: usually thousands), often multi-site.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient stable on digoxin starts a drug that inhibits P-glycoprotein (MDR1). What does the textbook predict?

options.A: Digoxin stops reaching tissues
options.B: Digoxin's therapeutic index widens
options.C: Digoxin blood levels rise
options.D: Digoxin becomes a prodrug
options.E: Digoxin blood levels fall

items.why: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) pumps drugs out of cells; inhibiting it increases blood levels of digoxin — dangerous for a narrow-TI drug.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A PA is choosing a starting dose for an individual patient. According to the textbook, which range is most useful?

options.A: The range from EC₅₀ up to Emax
options.B: The animal-derived TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ ratio
options.C: The range from LD₅₀ down to TD₅₀
options.D: The fraction of the dose absorbed
options.E: The therapeutic window

items.why: The therapeutic window — between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — is of greater practical value in choosing a dose for a patient.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What does the textbook mean by "spare receptors"?

options.A: New receptors made after long-term use
options.B: Receptors that bind only antagonist drugs
options.C: Receptors that bind drug irreversibly
options.D: Maximal response occurs without full receptor occupancy
options.E: Receptors that cannot bind any drug at all

items.why: Receptors are 'spare' when a maximal response can be produced without occupying all of them (e.g., ~90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response preserved).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which efflux transporter is found in the brain and testes and limits drug entry there?

options.A: CYP3A4
options.B: P-glycoprotein (MDR1)
options.C: TPMT
options.D: VKORC1
options.E: Plasma albumin

items.why: P-glycoprotein (MDR1), an ABC efflux transporter in the brain, testes, and other tissues, pumps drugs back out.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which route has a bioavailability of about 30% to <100% and less first-pass effect than oral dosing?

options.A: Rectal
options.B: Transdermal
options.C: Inhalation
options.D: Intramuscular
options.E: Intravenous

items.why: Rectal (PR): 30% to <100%, less first-pass effect than oral — about half of a rectal dose bypasses the liver.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A drug lowers blood pressure, whether or not that was the reason it was given. What is this measurable change called?

options.A: Drug toxicity
options.B: The drug's efficacy
options.C: An adverse drug reaction
options.D: A therapeutic effect
options.E: A pharmacologic effect

items.why: Pharmacologic effect = any measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient who drinks grapefruit juice daily has a higher level of a CYP3A4-substrate drug. What does the textbook say explains this?

options.A: Grapefruit lowers plasma protein binding
options.B: Grapefruit induces liver CYP3A4
options.C: Grapefruit binds the drug in the gut
options.D: Gut-wall CYP3A4 and P-gp are inhibited
options.E: Grapefruit speeds renal clearance

items.why: Grapefruit juice inhibits P-glycoprotein and gut-wall CYP3A4 metabolism, which can substantially increase drug absorption — first-pass loss can happen in the gut wall as well as the liver.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Under FDA rules, how soon must an adverse event that is both serious and unexpected be reported?

options.A: Within 90 days
options.B: Within 15 days
options.C: Within 7 days
options.D: Within 30 days
options.E: Within 24 hours

items.why: Events that are both serious and unexpected must be reported to the FDA within 15 days.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Phase I (CYP450): oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis. Phase II: conjugation → water-soluble.
items.back: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis. Phase II: conjugation → water-soluble.
items.cloze: Phase I (CYP450): {{c1::oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis}}. Phase II: {{c2::conjugation → water-soluble}}.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Inhibitor → substrate ↑ → toxicity; inducer → substrate ↓ → therapeutic failure.
items.back: substrate ↑ → toxicity; inducer → substrate ↓ → therapeutic failure.
items.cloze: Inhibitor → {{c1::substrate ↑ → toxicity}}; inducer → {{c2::substrate ↓ → therapeutic failure}}.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Narrow-TI substrate + CYP inhibitor = especially dangerous.
items.cloze: Narrow-TI substrate + CYP inhibitor = {{c1::especially dangerous}}.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Metabolism can produce toxic metabolites (e.g., NAPQI).
items.cloze: Metabolism can produce toxic metabolites (e.g., {{c1::NAPQI}}).

items.label: Definition
items.text: Drug metabolism = how the body chemically transforms drugs.
items.back: how the body chemically transforms drugs.
items.cloze: Drug metabolism = {{c1::how the body chemically transforms drugs}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Phase I — Functionalization: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis.
items.cloze: Phase I — Functionalization: {{c1::oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Phase II — Conjugation: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione conjugation.
items.back: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione conjugation.
items.cloze: Phase II — Conjugation: {{c1::glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione conjugation}}.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Enzyme inhibition: a drug slows a CYP enzyme, raising the blood level of any drug that CYP normally clears.
items.back: a drug slows a CYP enzyme, raising the blood level of any drug that CYP normally clears.
items.cloze: {{c1::Enzyme inhibition}}: a drug slows a CYP enzyme, raising the blood level of any drug that CYP normally clears.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Enzyme induction: a drug increases CYP enzyme production, lowering the blood level (and effect) of drugs that CYP clears.
items.back: a drug increases CYP enzyme production, lowering the blood level (and effect) of drugs that CYP clears.
items.cloze: {{c1::Enzyme induction}}: a drug increases CYP enzyme production, lowering the blood level (and effect) of drugs that CYP clears.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Cytochrome P450 (in the liver’s smooth endoplasmic reticulum) does most Phase I work and has low substrate specificity: lipid-soluble drugs are its common thread.
items.cloze: {{c1::Cytochrome P450}} (in the liver’s smooth endoplasmic reticulum) does most Phase I work and has low substrate specificity: lipid-soluble drugs are its common thread.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: CYP450 interactions are one of the highest-yield concepts in all of pharmacology — nearly every major drug class has at least one clinically important CYP interaction.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Example: Drug A inhibits CYP3A4 → Drug B (a CYP3A4 substrate) accumulates → toxicity risk rises.
items.back: Drug A inhibits CYP3A4 → Drug B (a CYP3A4 substrate) accumulates → toxicity risk rises.
items.cloze: Example: {{c1::Drug A inhibits CYP3A4 → Drug B (a CYP3A4 substrate) accumulates → toxicity risk rises}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Inhibition pushes a substrate's level ABOVE 100% of baseline (toxicity risk); induction pushes it BELOW 100% (therapeutic-failure risk).
items.cloze: Inhibition pushes a substrate's level ABOVE {{c1::100%}} of baseline (toxicity risk); induction pushes it BELOW 100% (therapeutic-failure risk).

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Inhibiting the CYP that clears a substrate is especially dangerous when the substrate has a narrow therapeutic index.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis) slows metabolism enough that ordinary doses can cause coma. CYP3A4 handles over 50% of liver-metabolized prescriptions.
items.cloze: Liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis) slows metabolism enough that ordinary doses can cause coma. CYP3A4 handles over {{c1::50%}} of liver-metabolized prescriptions.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Diet and environment: smoking, charcoal-broiled food and cruciferous vegetables induce CYP1A; grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A.
items.back: smoking, charcoal-broiled food and cruciferous vegetables induce CYP1A; grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A.
items.cloze: {{c1::Diet and environment}}: smoking, charcoal-broiled food and cruciferous vegetables induce CYP1A; grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Stopping an inducer is as risky as starting one: when the inducer stops, warfarin metabolism slows, levels rise and bleeding can follow.
items.front: Stopping an inducer is as risky as starting one
items.back: when the inducer stops, warfarin metabolism slows, levels rise and bleeding can follow.
items.cloze: Stopping an inducer is as risky as starting one: {{c1::when the inducer stops, warfarin metabolism slows, levels rise and bleeding can follow}}.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Inhibitor → substrate level UP (toxicity); inducer → substrate level DOWN (therapeutic failure). Don't swap them.
items.back: substrate level UP (toxicity); inducer → substrate level DOWN (therapeutic failure). Don't swap them.
items.cloze: Inhibitor → {{c1::substrate level UP (toxicity)}}; inducer → {{c2::substrate level DOWN (therapeutic failure)}}. Don't swap them.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: CYP3A4 is a Phase I (CYP450) enzyme — it does not "only affect Phase II metabolism."
items.front: CYP3A4 is a Phase I (CYP450) enzyme …
items.back: it does not "only affect Phase II metabolism."
items.cloze: CYP3A4 is a Phase I (CYP450) enzyme … {{c1::it does not "only affect Phase II metabolism."}}

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Not every drug goes through Phase I first — some go straight to Phase II conjugation.
items.front: Not every drug goes through Phase I first …
items.back: some go straight to Phase II conjugation.
items.cloze: Not every drug goes through Phase I first … {{c1::some go straight to Phase II conjugation}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Why metabolize? To inactivate an active drug, making it easier to excrete.
items.back: To inactivate an active drug, making it easier to excrete.
items.cloze: Why metabolize? {{c1::To inactivate an active drug, making it easier to excrete}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: To activate a prodrug into its active form.

items.label: How it works
items.text: To produce an active metabolite that contributes to (or extends) the drug effect.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Occasionally to produce a toxic metabolite — the basis of some drug-induced organ injury.
items.front: Occasionally to produce a toxic metabolite …
items.back: the basis of some drug-induced organ injury.
items.cloze: Occasionally to produce a toxic metabolite … {{c1::the basis of some drug-induced organ injury}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase I is primarily carried out by cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes and often creates or unmasks a reactive functional group.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase II attaches a polar group to the molecule, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always — some drugs go straight to conjugation.
items.front: Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always …
items.back: some drugs go straight to conjugation.
items.cloze: Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always … {{c1::some drugs go straight to conjugation}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Inhibition slows clearance (substrate level rises); induction speeds clearance (substrate level falls).

items.label: How it works
items.text: Acetaminophen is mostly conjugated (glucuronide/sulfate); in overdose glutathione is depleted and the toxic metabolite (NAPQI) injures the liver — N-acetylcysteine given within 8–16 hours protects against fulminant hepatotoxicity.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Half-life is determined by clearance and volume of distribution together — it is not a fixed drug "property" independent of physiology.

items.label: How it works
items.text: A drug is roughly 97% eliminated after about 5 half-lives.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Formula: % remaining = 100% x (1/2)^(number of half-life) — i.e., per number of half-lives elapsed.
items.back: % remaining = 100% x (1/2)^(number of half-life) — i.e., per number of half-lives elapsed.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Formula: C(t) = C₀ x (1/2)^(t/t½) — C₀ = starting concentration, t = time elapsed.
items.back: C(t) = C₀ x (1/2)^(t/t½) — C₀ = starting concentration, t = time elapsed.
items.cloze: {{c1::Formula: C(t) = C₀ x (1/2)^(t/t½)}} — C₀ = starting concentration, t = time elapsed.

items.text: Worked example (both formulas): t½ = 6 h; an IV dose gives a starting plasma concentration of 100 mg/L — see the table for each half-life.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Clearance determines how efficiently a drug is removed — and, along with Vd, determines half-life.

items.text: Total clearance is usually the sum of hepatic and renal clearance.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Steady state takes ~4–5 half-lives regardless of dose size — the same reason a drug is ~97% eliminated ~5 half-lives after stopping it.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life.
items.cloze: Time to steady state (about 4–{{c1::5 half-lives}}) is governed by half-life.

items.label: How it works
items.text: During regular dosing: 50% of steady state after 1 half-life, 75% after 2, and over 90% after 4 — the textbook's "four half-lives" rule of thumb.
items.back: 50% of steady state after 1 half-life, 75% after 2, and over 90% after 4 — the textbook's "four half-lives" rule of thumb.
items.cloze: During regular dosing: {{c1::50%}} of steady state after 1 half-life, {{c2::75%}} after 2, and over {{c3::90%}} after 4 — the textbook's "four half-lives" rule of thumb.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Capacity-limited (saturable) elimination: clearance falls as concentration rises — important for phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin.
items.back: clearance falls as concentration rises — important for phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin.
items.cloze: {{c1::Capacity-limited (saturable) elimination}}: clearance falls as concentration rises — important for phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Maintenance dosing rate = clearance × target concentration (÷ F if oral). The dosing interval changes only peaks and troughs, not the average level.
items.back: clearance × target concentration (÷ F if oral). The dosing interval changes only peaks and troughs, not the average level.
items.cloze: {{c1::Maintenance dosing rate = clearance × target concentration}} (÷ F if oral). The dosing interval changes only peaks and troughs, not the average level.

items.text: Half-life can change without clearance changing: diazepam’s half-life lengthens with age because its Vd grows.

items.back: diazepam’s half-life lengthens with age because its Vd grows.

items.text: Effects can outlast plasma levels (delayed effects): warfarin acts only as clotting factors turn over.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Agonist or antagonist? A new drug binds the same receptor as a home medication, and the home medication's effect weakens. Is the new drug most likely a competitive antagonist, and how could you confirm it pharmacologically?
items.back: A new drug binds the same receptor as a home medication, and the home medication's effect weakens. Is the new drug most likely a competitive antagonist, and how could you confirm it pharmacologically?

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Clinical pearl: a competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — if raising the home medication's dose restores the effect, that supports competitive (rather than irreversible) antagonism.
items.back: a competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — if raising the home medication's dose restores the effect, that supports competitive (rather than irreversible) antagonism.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Study-guide case: 68-year-old woman, stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min), starting a narrow-TI oral antiarrhythmic eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney; she started a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor 3 weeks ago.
items.back: 68-year-old woman, stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min), starting a narrow-TI oral antiarrhythmic eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney; she started a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor 3 weeks ago.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Two concerns: reduced renal clearance from CKD will raise the antiarrhythmic's concentration and prolong its half-life regardless of the new drug; separately, if it has any hepatic/CYP3A4 component, the CYP3A4 inhibitor would compound accumulation further.
items.back: reduced renal clearance from CKD will raise the antiarrhythmic's concentration and prolong its half-life regardless of the new drug; separately, if it has any hepatic/CYP3A4 component, the CYP3A4 inhibitor would compound accumulation further.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Before dispensing: check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and closely monitor renal function and signs of toxicity (arrhythmia worsening, other drug-specific toxicity) after starting.
items.back: check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and closely monitor renal function and signs of toxicity (arrhythmia worsening, other drug-specific toxicity) after starting.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: If the drug were instead cleared by the liver via CYP3A4: the direct renal-clearance concern becomes less central (though CKD can still indirectly affect hepatic drug handling), and the CYP3A4 interaction becomes the dominant concern.
