items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 6, the "+ Enzyme inhibitor" bar rises to 240% of baseline, while the "+ Enzyme inducer" bar falls to 42%. For a patient on a stable dose of the substrate drug, which condition poses the greatest risk of toxicity?

options.A: Normal metabolism
options.B: Enzyme induction
options.C: Neither condition changes risk
options.D: Enzyme inhibition — because it raises the substrate drug’s blood level

items.why: The tallest bar in the chart is the enzyme-inhibitor condition at 240% of baseline — the substrate drug accumulates because it can no longer be cleared normally, raising toxicity risk. The inducer bar shows the opposite problem (42%, risking therapeutic failure), not toxicity.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient stable on a CYP3A4-substrate medication with a narrow therapeutic index is started on a new drug that is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: No change, since CYP3A4 only affects Phase II metabolism
options.B: Decreased substrate drug level and reduced effect
options.C: Increased substrate drug level and increased toxicity risk
options.D: Increased renal clearance of the substrate drug

items.why: Inhibiting the CYP enzyme responsible for clearing the substrate drug slows its metabolism, raising its blood level — especially dangerous when the substrate has a narrow therapeutic index.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient’s eGFR drops significantly due to new chronic kidney disease. For a drug that is primarily renally eliminated, what dosing adjustment is most appropriate?

options.A: No adjustment is needed
options.B: Increase the dose
options.C: Switch to IV administration only
options.D: Decrease the dose and/or extend the dosing interval

items.why: Reduced renal clearance raises drug exposure for renally-eliminated drugs; the standard response is a lower dose, a longer interval, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Using Figure 7, approximately what percentage of the original drug concentration remains after 3 half-lives (3 t½)?
items.why: Each half-life cuts the remaining concentration in half: 100% → 50% (1 t½) → 25% (2 t½) → 12.5% (3 t½), exactly as marked on the curve. By 5 half-lives the drug is roughly 97% eliminated (about 3% remaining).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 8, the dashed orange line (loading dose + maintenance) starts at the target concentration immediately, while the solid teal line (maintenance only) climbs gradually over several doses. What is the clinical advantage of adding a loading dose?

options.A: It permanently lowers the maintenance dose needed
options.B: It eliminates the need for monitoring
options.C: It has no advantage over maintenance dosing alone
options.D: It reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives

items.why: The dashed loading-dose curve starts at the dotted steady-state line from the very first dose, while the solid maintenance-only curve needs several dosing intervals (~4–5 half-lives) to climb to that same level — exactly as defined on the previous slide. A loading dose does not change the maintenance dose itself or remove the need for monitoring.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Approximately how many half-lives are required for a drug to reach steady state with regular, repeated dosing?

options.D: Steady state is reached immediately after the first dose

items.why: Steady state — where drug intake equals drug elimination — is reached in roughly 4–5 half-lives, regardless of dose size. This is also why a drug is roughly 97% eliminated about 5 half-lives after stopping it.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient is found to carry the HLA-B*5801 allele before starting allopurinol. Why does this matter clinically?

options.A: It identifies a sharply increased risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction
options.B: It predicts reduced drug absorption
options.C: It only affects how the drug tastes
options.D: It has no bearing on drug selection

items.why: HLA-B*5801 is associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol — a textbook pharmacogenomic screening consideration you will see again in Thursday’s gout lecture.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Before prescribing any new medication, which single check is most directly aimed at preventing a toxic, often-predictable drug-drug interaction?

options.A: Confirming the drug’s brand name
options.B: Checking the drug’s chemical name
options.C: Reviewing the drug’s half-life alone
options.D: Reviewing CYP450 interactions with the patient’s current medications

items.why: CYP450 interaction screening is one of the single highest-yield steps for preventing predictable, preventable toxicity before adding any new drug to a regimen.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A drug has high potency but low efficacy compared to an alternative. For a patient needing maximum symptom relief, which factor matters more when choosing between the two?

options.A: Efficacy
options.B: Potency
options.C: Both matter equally
options.D: Neither predicts clinical benefit

items.why: Efficacy (the maximum achievable effect) matters more than potency for most clinical outcomes.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with CKD is prescribed a renally-cleared, narrow-TI drug without dose adjustment. Which two consequences would you expect together?

options.A: Decreased half-life and decreased concentration
options.B: Increased clearance and decreased Vd
options.C: Increased half-life and increased concentration
options.D: No change in either parameter

items.why: Reduced renal clearance raises both drug concentration and half-life.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which best differentiates a competitive antagonist from a noncompetitive antagonist?

options.A: Competitive lowers Emax; noncompetitive does not
options.B: Noncompetitive lowers Emax; competitive shifts the curve right without changing Emax
options.C: They are pharmacologically identical
options.D: Only competitive antagonists cause adverse effects

items.why: Noncompetitive/irreversible antagonists lower Emax; competitive antagonists shift the curve right without changing Emax.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Drug A, a CYP enzyme inducer, is started in a patient taking Drug B, a substrate of that same CYP enzyme. What happens to Drug B’s level and effect?

options.A: Increases, raising toxicity risk
options.B: No change
options.C: Drug B’s route of elimination changes to biliary
options.D: Decreases, risking therapeutic failure

items.why: Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A narrow-therapeutic-index medication requires monitoring. Which pharmacokinetic parameter most directly determines how long it takes to reach steady-state concentration?

options.A: Half-life
options.B: Bioavailability
options.C: Route of administration
options.D: Chemical name

items.why: Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A PA reviews indication, contraindications, renal/hepatic function, interactions, and a monitoring plan before prescribing. This process best reflects:

options.A: Pharmacogenomic testing
options.B: Receptor pharmacology alone
options.C: The clinical decision-making framework
options.D: Phase IV surveillance

items.why: This checklist is the clinical decision-making framework from the "Putting It All Together" section.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A drug undergoes glucuronidation, which attaches a polar group to the molecule. Which statement best describes this step?

options.A: A Phase I oxidation that unmasks a reactive functional group on the drug
options.B: A CYP450-driven hydrolysis that always precedes any Phase II reaction
options.C: A Phase II reaction that makes the drug more lipophilic and longer-acting
options.D: A Phase II conjugation that makes the drug more water-soluble for excretion
options.E: A reduction reaction that converts a prodrug into its active form

items.why: Glucuronidation is a Phase II (conjugation) reaction that attaches a polar group, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion (S5).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 19-year-old arrives 6 hours after a large intentional acetaminophen ingestion. Labs are pending. Which treatment best protects against fulminant liver injury?

options.A: Sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine and speed excretion
options.B: N-acetylcysteine, started within the 8–16 hour window
options.C: Protamine to bind and neutralize the circulating drug
options.D: Rifampin to induce CYP enzymes and clear the drug faster
options.E: Waiting for levels before giving any treatment at all

items.why: N-acetylcysteine given within 8–16 hours protects against acetaminophen hepatotoxicity by replacing depleted glutathione (p. 66).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A heavy smoker on a CYP1A2-metabolized drug quits smoking abruptly. What should the PA anticipate?

options.A: No change, since smoking affects only the lungs
options.B: Drug levels will fall because metabolism speeds up
options.C: The drug becomes a prodrug that needs activation
options.D: Drug levels may rise as CYP1A induction fades
options.E: Renal clearance will double right away

items.why: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A; when the inducer stops, metabolism slows and levels can rise (p. 60; p. 72).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient arrives after an aspirin overdose, and the team alkalinizes the urine. How does this increase elimination of the drug?

options.A: It shifts elimination from the kidney to bile and feces
options.B: It makes the drug more lipophilic so it is reabsorbed
options.C: It increases glomerular filtration of protein-bound drug
options.D: It activates tubular transporters that secrete the drug
options.E: It traps ionized drug in the tubule, blocking its reabsorption

items.why: Urine pH manipulation works by trapping ionized drug in the tubule, blocking reabsorption (S14 notes); only lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed (S14).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which renal process REDUCES the net elimination of a drug?

options.A: Tubular secretion by active transporters
options.B: Passive reabsorption of lipophilic, un-ionized drug
options.C: Excretion of volatile agents by the lungs
options.D: Filtration of drug based on molecular size
options.E: Glomerular filtration of free, unbound drug

items.why: Tubular reabsorption: lipophilic, un-ionized drug passively diffuses back into the blood, reducing net elimination (S14).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient receives an IV dose that gives a starting plasma concentration of 100 mg/L. The drug's half-life is 6 hours. What is the plasma concentration at 18 hours?

options.A: 6.25 mg/L, with 93.75% of the drug eliminated
options.B: 25 mg/L, with 75% of the drug eliminated
options.C: 12.5 mg/L, with 87.5% of the drug eliminated
options.D: 3.125 mg/L, with about 97% eliminated
options.E: 50 mg/L, with 50% of the drug eliminated

items.why: 18 h = 3 half-lives: C(t) = 100 × (1/2)^3 = 12.5 mg/L (87.5% eliminated) (S19).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which statement correctly pairs each dose type with the parameter it is based on?

options.A: Loading dose is based on bioavailability; maintenance dose on Vd
options.B: Loading dose is based on Vd; maintenance dose is based on clearance
options.C: Both loading and maintenance doses are based on clearance alone
options.D: Loading dose is based on clearance; maintenance dose is based on Vd
options.E: Both loading and maintenance doses are based on half-life alone

items.why: Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance (S23 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A drug is given every 8 hours instead of every 24 hours, keeping the same total daily dose. What happens to its average steady-state concentration?

options.A: It depends on Vd, which now changes
options.B: It triples because doses come more often
options.C: It falls because each dose is smaller
options.D: It stays the same; only peaks and troughs change
options.E: It doubles because half-life gets longer

items.why: The average steady-state level depends only on dosing rate and clearance; the interval changes only the swings (p. 51).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient is about to start azathioprine. Testing shows TPMT deficiency. What is the main clinical concern?

options.A: Reduced activation of the drug into its active form
options.B: Faster CYP2D6 metabolism of the drug and lost effect
options.C: Increased risk of toxicity from the thiopurine drug
options.D: Severe HLA-associated hypersensitivity to the drug
options.E: No concern, since genotype never affects therapy

items.why: TPMT deficiency raises toxicity risk with thiopurine drugs such as azathioprine (S33).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which pairing of a genetic variant with the drug it most affects is correct?

options.A: CYP2C19 variation — allopurinol reactions
options.B: CYP2D6 variation — azathioprine toxicity
options.C: HLA-B*5801 — clopidogrel activation
options.D: CYP2C19 variation — clopidogrel activation
options.E: TPMT variation — codeine activation

items.why: CYP2C19 variation affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing (S33).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which statement about using pharmacogenomic results best matches the lecture's personalized-pharmacotherapy model?

options.A: Genotype affects adverse-reaction risk but never drug metabolism
options.B: Genotype alone should determine both the drug and its dose
options.C: Genotype becomes irrelevant once a drug reaches steady state
options.D: Genotype matters only for drugs that are given by the IV route
options.E: Genotype is one input alongside phenotype, disease, and other drugs

items.why: Pharmacogenomics is one input among several — genotype alone never dictates therapy in isolation (S34).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 62-year-old has a coronary stent placed. Genotyping shows he is a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer. Which antiplatelet choice does CPIC guidance support?

options.A: Prasugrel or ticagrelor instead of clopidogrel
options.B: Azathioprine at 30–70% of the usual starting dose
options.C: Clopidogrel at the standard dose with routine follow-up
options.D: Clopidogrel plus a CYP2C19 inhibitor to raise its level
options.E: Codeine-free analgesia plus standard-dose clopidogrel

items.why: Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 activation; poor metabolizers make little active drug, so prasugrel or ticagrelor is recommended (p. 81; p. 82).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient starts a new drug that binds the same receptor as their home medication, and the home medication's effect becomes weaker. Raising the home medication's dose restores the full effect. What does this support?

options.A: The new drug is a strong CYP3A4 inducer
options.B: The new drug is an irreversible antagonist
options.C: The home medication has become toxic
options.D: The new drug is a competitive antagonist
options.E: The new drug is a full agonist itself

items.why: A competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — restoring the effect supports competitive rather than irreversible antagonism (S41).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min) is starting a narrow-TI oral antiarrhythmic eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney. Three weeks ago she began a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What is the best step before the prescription is filled?

options.A: Shorten the dosing interval so steady state is reached more quickly
options.B: Prescribe the standard dose, since only hepatic drugs are affected by CKD
options.C: Increase the dose, since the CYP3A4 inhibitor will lower the drug's level
options.D: Start the drug, and check renal function only if symptoms appear later
options.E: Check eGFR/CrCl, lower the dose or extend the interval, and plan close monitoring

items.why: Reduced renal clearance will raise the drug's concentration and prolong its half-life; before dispensing, check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and monitor renal function and toxicity (SG U1-S).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient stops taking a drug. About how many half-lives until it is roughly 97% eliminated?

options.A: About 5 half-lives
options.B: About 2 half-lives
options.C: About 10 half-lives
options.D: About 3 half-lives
options.E: About 1 half-life

items.why: A drug is roughly 97% eliminated after about 5 half-lives (3.125% remains).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on a CYP3A4 substrate starts a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. What should you watch for clinically?

options.A: Higher oral bioavailability of the inhibitor
options.B: Faster renal clearance of the substrate
options.C: Loss of effect from falling substrate levels
options.D: A shorter half-life of the substrate
options.E: Signs of toxicity from rising substrate levels

items.why: Inhibiting the CYP that clears the substrate raises its level — always check CYP interactions before adding a drug; one of the most preventable causes of toxicity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Before allopurinol, a patient tests positive for HLA-B*5801. Why does it matter?

options.A: Predicts reduced absorption of allopurinol
options.B: Sharply higher risk of severe hypersensitivity
options.C: Predicts faster CYP2D6 metabolism of the drug
options.D: Predicts higher thiopurine toxicity risk
options.E: Has no bearing on drug selection here

items.why: HLA-B*5801 is associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol — a textbook pharmacogenomic screening consideration.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement about the order of metabolism phases is correct?

options.A: Phase II must always follow Phase I
options.B: Phase II occurs only in the kidney
options.C: Phase I always follows Phase II
options.D: Phase I often comes first, but not always
options.E: Every drug undergoes both phases

items.why: Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always — some drugs go straight to conjugation.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which parameter most directly determines the time to reach steady state?

options.A: The drug's half-life
options.B: The route of administration
options.C: The size of each dose
options.D: The drug's bioavailability
options.E: The drug's chemical name

items.why: Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement matches the lecture's personalized-pharmacotherapy model?

options.A: Genotype is irrelevant at steady state
options.B: Genotype alone should decide the drug
options.C: Genotype affects ADRs but not metabolism
options.D: Genotype is one input among several
options.E: Genotype matters only for IV drugs

items.why: Pharmacogenomics is one input among several — genotype, phenotype, disease state, and other medications combine into individualized therapy.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient takes a large, highly protein-bound drug. Which elimination route did the lecture call important for such drugs?

options.A: The lungs
options.B: Sweat glands
options.C: The kidney
options.D: Bile and feces
options.E: Breast milk

items.why: Bile/feces: important for some large or protein-bound drugs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A PA reviews indication, contraindications, renal/hepatic function, interactions, and monitoring before prescribing. What is this?

options.A: Receptor pharmacology considered alone
options.B: Phase IV postmarketing surveillance
options.C: Pharmacogenomic screening of the patient
options.D: Therapeutic index testing of the drug
options.E: The clinical decision-making framework

items.why: This checklist is the clinical decision-making framework from 'Putting It All Together.'

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which reactions belong to Phase I (functionalization) metabolism?

options.A: Glucuronidation, sulfation, and acetylation
options.B: Oxidation, sulfation, and hydrolysis
options.C: Methylation, oxidation, and glutathione conjugation
options.D: Reduction, acetylation, and glucuronidation
options.E: Oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis

items.why: Phase I — functionalization: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; primarily by CYP450 enzymes.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A CKD patient takes a renally cleared, narrow-TI drug without dose adjustment. Which two changes occur?

options.A: Half-life falls and concentration rises
options.B: Neither half-life nor concentration changes
options.C: Half-life rises and concentration rises
options.D: Clearance rises and Vd falls
options.E: Half-life falls and concentration falls

items.why: Reduced renal clearance raises drug concentration and prolongs half-life.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which is NOT one of the lecture's purposes of drug metabolism?

options.A: Increasing a drug's lipid solubility for storage
options.B: Producing an active metabolite that extends effect
options.C: Occasionally producing a toxic metabolite
options.D: Inactivating an active drug for excretion
options.E: Activating a prodrug into its active form

items.why: Metabolism inactivates drugs, activates prodrugs, makes active metabolites, and occasionally toxic metabolites — it makes drugs easier to excrete, not more lipid-soluble for storage.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient about to start azathioprine has TPMT deficiency. What is the main concern?

options.A: Faster CYP2D6 metabolism and lost effect
options.B: No concern, since genotype never matters
options.C: Increased toxicity risk from the thiopurine
options.D: Reduced activation of the drug
options.E: Severe HLA-linked hypersensitivity to the drug

items.why: TPMT deficiency raises toxicity risk with thiopurine drugs (e.g., azathioprine).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which sequence matches the lecture's integrated pharmacology pathway?

options.A: Dose → absorption → excretion → target → effect
options.B: Dose → target → absorption → distribution → effect
options.C: Dose → absorption → distribution → target → effect
options.D: Dose → distribution → absorption → target → effect
options.E: Dose → metabolism → absorption → target → effect

items.why: One integrated pathway: Dose → Absorption → Distribution → Receptor/Target → Effect, with Metabolism and Excretion clearing the drug.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A PA must adjust a renally cleared drug for a patient with CKD. Which bedside estimates of renal function guide the adjustment?

options.A: Serum drug level and half-life
options.B: TPMT activity and CYP2D6 status
options.C: eGFR and creatinine clearance (CrCl)
options.D: Volume of distribution and EC₅₀
options.E: Bioavailability and first-pass effect

items.why: eGFR and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard bedside estimates of renal function used to adjust dosing.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An IV dose gives 100 mg/L; the half-life is 6 hours. What is the concentration at 18 hours?

options.A: 25 mg/L
options.C: 50 mg/L

items.why: 18 h = 3 half-lives: C(t) = 100 x (1/2)^3 = 12.5 mg/L (87.5% eliminated).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which is the dominant elimination route for most drugs and their metabolites?

options.A: Sweat glands
options.B: Breast milk
options.C: The lungs
options.D: The kidney
options.E: Bile and feces

items.why: The kidney is the dominant route for most drugs and metabolites.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: How is clearance defined?

options.A: Point where intake equals elimination
options.B: Time for plasma level to fall by half
options.C: Fraction of a dose reaching circulation
options.D: Plasma volume fully cleared of drug per time
options.E: Total drug relative to plasma level

items.why: Clearance = the volume of plasma from which drug is completely removed per unit time.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient is starting clopidogrel. Variation in which gene affects its activation?

options.A: CYP3A4
options.B: TPMT
options.C: CYP2D6
options.D: CYP2C19
options.E: HLA-B*5801

items.why: CYP2C19 variation affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which parameters are loading and maintenance doses based on?

options.A: Both based on clearance alone
options.B: Loading on Vd; maintenance on clearance
options.C: Both based on half-life alone
options.D: Loading on bioavailability; maintenance on Vd
options.E: Loading on clearance; maintenance on Vd

items.why: Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient's eGFR drops with new CKD. How should a primarily renally eliminated drug be adjusted?

options.A: Switch to IV administration only
options.B: Shorten the dosing interval instead
options.C: Make no adjustment to dose or interval
options.D: Raise the dose to maintain the effect
options.E: Lower the dose and/or extend the interval

items.why: Reduced renal clearance raises exposure; respond with a lower dose, a longer interval, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which two parameters together determine half-life?

options.A: Clearance and volume of distribution
options.B: Vd and the therapeutic index
options.C: Bioavailability and potency
options.D: Dose size and dosing route
options.E: Clearance and bioavailability

items.why: Half-life is determined by clearance and Vd together — not a fixed drug property independent of physiology.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: In the lecture's figure, an inhibitor raises a substrate to 240% of baseline and an inducer lowers it to 42%. Which poses toxicity risk?

options.A: Neither, since both are within range
options.B: The inducer, lowering the level to 42%
options.C: The inhibitor, raising the level to 240%
options.D: Both equally, since any change is toxic
options.E: Baseline, since it is the reference level

items.why: The inhibitor bar (240%) shows the substrate accumulating because it can't be cleared normally; the inducer (42%) risks failure instead.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient overdoses on acetaminophen, and normal Phase I metabolism produces NAPQI. What is NAPQI an example of?

options.A: A prodrug activated by Phase II
options.B: An inactive Phase II conjugate
options.C: An efflux pump at the blood-brain barrier
options.D: A CYP3A4 inhibitor used clinically
options.E: A toxic metabolite from normal metabolism

items.why: NAPQI (from acetaminophen) is the textbook example of a toxic metabolite produced by normal Phase I metabolism.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A breastfeeding patient asks about a new drug. Why does breast milk, a minor elimination route, still matter here?

options.A: It matters for lactating patients
options.B: It traps ionized drug in urine
options.C: It handles large protein-bound drugs
options.D: It is the dominant route for most drugs
options.E: It clears volatile anesthetic gases

items.why: Sweat and breast milk are minor routes, but breast milk matters for lactating patients.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L02 S41; L01 S22; SG U1-M
items.stem: A new drug weakens a patient's home medication at the same receptor; raising the home dose restores the full effect. What is the new drug?

options.A: A noncompetitive antagonist
options.B: A partial agonist
options.C: A competitive antagonist
options.D: An inverse agonist
options.E: An irreversible antagonist

items.why: A competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — restoring the effect supports competitive rather than irreversible antagonism.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: About what percentage of the original concentration remains after 3 half-lives?
items.why: Each half-life halves what remains: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5% after 3 t½.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why are CYP450 interactions considered one of the highest-yield concepts?

options.A: They cannot be predicted before prescribing
options.B: They affect only the IV route of dosing
options.C: Nearly every drug class has an important one
options.D: They occur only with narrow-TI drugs
options.E: They are limited to Phase II metabolism

items.why: Nearly every major drug class has at least one clinically important CYP interaction.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which renal process reduces a drug's net elimination?

options.A: Reabsorption of lipophilic, un-ionized drug
options.B: Filtration of free, unbound drug
options.C: Secretion by active transporters
options.D: Exhalation of volatile anesthetic gases
options.E: Filtration based on molecular size

items.why: Tubular reabsorption: lipophilic, un-ionized drug passively diffuses back into the blood, reducing net elimination.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What is the main result of Phase II conjugation?

options.A: Activation of a prodrug by CYP450 enzymes
options.B: A more water-soluble product for excretion
options.C: A more lipophilic product for reabsorption
options.D: Unmasking of a reactive functional group
options.E: A larger Vd from tissue sequestration

items.why: Phase II attaches a polar group, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which item is NOT on the lecture's before-you-prescribe checklist?

options.A: Renal and hepatic function
options.B: Drug interactions, including CYP450
options.C: Contraindications and allergies
options.D: The drug's brand name
options.E: Age, pregnancy, and patient factors

items.why: Checklist: indication; contraindications and allergies; renal and hepatic function; drug interactions (incl. CYP450); age, pregnancy, patient factors; correct dose, route, and monitoring plan.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient starts a regularly dosed medication with no loading dose. About how many half-lives until steady state?

options.A: About 8–10 half-lives
options.B: About 2–3 half-lives
options.C: About 4–5 half-lives
options.D: About 1–2 half-lives
options.E: Right after the first dose

items.why: Steady state — intake equals elimination — is reached in roughly 4–5 half-lives, regardless of dose size.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with worsening renal impairment takes several medicines. Which renally cleared, narrow-TI drugs did the lecture flag for adjustment?

options.A: Many antibiotics, digoxin, and morphine
options.B: Many antibiotics, digoxin, and lithium
options.C: Many antibiotics, heparin, and lithium
options.D: Albuterol, digoxin, and lithium
options.E: Many antibiotics, digoxin, and propranolol

items.why: Any renally-cleared, narrow-TI drug (many antibiotics, digoxin, lithium) needs a dose or interval adjustment in renal impairment.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Drug A, a CYP inducer, is started in a patient on Drug B, a substrate of that enzyme. What happens to Drug B?

options.A: Its level is unchanged by enzyme induction
options.B: Its level rises, raising toxicity risk
options.C: Its elimination route shifts to biliary
options.D: Its level falls, risking therapeutic failure
options.E: Its level rises, then falls to baseline

items.why: Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient needs a therapeutic drug level right away, so a loading dose is added. What is the clinical advantage?

options.A: Shortening the drug's half-life for good
options.B: Removing the need for drug-level monitoring
options.C: No real advantage over maintenance alone
options.D: Permanently lowering the maintenance dose
options.E: Reaching target immediately, not after 4–5 t½

items.why: A loading dose reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which renal process passes free drug from blood into the tubule based on molecular size?

options.A: Biliary excretion
options.B: Hepatic conjugation
options.C: Glomerular filtration
options.D: Tubular secretion
options.E: Tubular reabsorption

items.why: Glomerular filtration: free (unbound) drug passes from blood into the tubule based on molecular size.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which chain correctly follows reduced renal clearance?

options.A: t½ unchanged → time to steady state unchanged → none
options.B: t½ ↑ → time to steady state ↓ → accumulation
options.C: t½ ↓ → time to steady state ↑ → failure
options.D: t½ ↓ → time to steady state ↓ → accumulation
options.E: t½ ↑ → time to steady state ↑ → accumulation

items.why: Clearance down → half-life up → time to steady state up → accumulation risk up if the regimen isn't adjusted.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient is prescribed codeine. Variation in which enzyme alters codeine activation (and many antidepressants)?

options.A: CYP3A4
options.B: CYP2D6
options.C: HLA-B*5801
options.D: CYP2C19
options.E: TPMT

items.why: CYP2D6 variation alters metabolism of many antidepressants and opioids (e.g., codeine activation).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: After an aspirin overdose, the team alkalinizes the urine. How does this increase elimination?

options.A: It makes the drug lipophilic for reabsorption
options.B: It traps ionized drug, blocking reabsorption
options.C: It boosts filtration of protein-bound drug
options.D: It shifts elimination to bile and feces
options.E: It activates secretion by tubular transporters

items.why: Urine pH manipulation (alkalinizing urine in aspirin overdose) traps ionized drug in the tubule, blocking reabsorption.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which can genetic variation alter, according to the lecture?

options.A: Metabolism, transport, target, and response
options.B: Only drug metabolism by CYP enzymes
options.C: Only adverse reactions, not efficacy
options.D: Only drug transport across membranes
options.E: Only the drug's chemical structure

items.why: Genetic variation can alter drug metabolism (CYP activity), transport, target structure/expression, and overall response and ADR risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Total clearance is usually the sum of which two components?

options.A: Renal and pulmonary absorption
options.B: Hepatic and biliary absorption
options.C: Renal clearance and Vd
options.D: Hepatic and renal clearance
options.E: Hepatic clearance and half-life

items.why: Total clearance is usually the sum of hepatic and renal clearance.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient stable on a narrow-TI CYP3A4 substrate starts a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What happens?

options.A: No change, since CYP3A4 is a Phase II enzyme
options.B: Substrate level rises, raising toxicity risk
options.C: Substrate level rises, lowering toxicity risk
options.D: Substrate level falls, risking therapeutic failure
options.E: Renal clearance of the substrate rises sharply

items.why: Inhibiting the CYP that clears the substrate slows its metabolism and raises its level — especially dangerous with a narrow TI.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Before adding any new drug, which single check most directly prevents a predictable toxic interaction?

options.A: Review CYP450 interactions with current drugs
options.B: Review the new drug's half-life by itself
options.C: Confirm the drug's brand name with the patient
options.D: Confirm the route written on the order
options.E: Check the drug's chemical name in a reference

items.why: CYP450 interaction screening is one of the highest-yield steps for preventing predictable, preventable toxicity.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: After surgery, an inhaled anesthetic gas leaves the body mainly through which route?

options.A: The kidneys
options.B: The lungs
options.C: Bile and feces
options.D: Sweat
options.E: Breast milk

items.why: Lungs eliminate volatile agents such as anesthetic gases.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on lithium develops worsening chronic kidney disease. What is the safest plan?

options.A: Lower the dose or extend the interval and check levels
options.B: Raise the dose to maintain the effect
options.C: Stop monitoring since levels are predictable
options.D: Switch to IV lithium to bypass the kidney
options.E: Keep the dose, since lithium is liver-cleared

items.why: Renally cleared, narrow-TI drugs (lithium, digoxin, many antibiotics) need a dose or interval adjustment in renal impairment, guided by eGFR/CrCl, with blood levels.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A drug has a Vd of 70 L and a clearance of 7 L/h. Using t½ = 0.7 × Vd ÷ CL, what is its half-life?

options.A: 0.7 hours
options.B: 7 hours
options.C: 49 hours
options.D: 70 hours
options.E: 10 hours

items.why: t½ = 0.7 × Vd ÷ CL = 0.7 × 70 ÷ 7 = 7 hours. Half-life rises when Vd rises or clearance falls.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient who is a CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizer is prescribed codeine. What is the main concern?

options.A: Too little morphine forms, so no pain relief
options.B: Thiopurine toxicity from low TPMT
options.C: Codeine cannot be absorbed by mouth
options.D: Too much morphine forms, risking toxicity
options.E: Severe HLA-linked hypersensitivity

items.why: CYP2D6 converts codeine to morphine (about 200× more potent); ultrarapid metabolizers make too much morphine. CPIC recommends an alternative analgesic for ultrarapid and poor metabolizers.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement describes Phase I metabolism?

options.A: It often creates or unmasks a reactive group
options.B: It makes a drug less water-soluble for storage
options.C: It is carried out mainly by TPMT
options.D: It attaches a polar group such as glucuronide
options.E: It always follows Phase II conjugation

items.why: Phase I (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; mainly CYP450) often creates or unmasks a reactive functional group; Phase II then attaches a polar group.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on an oral contraceptive starts St. John's wort for low mood. What is the main risk?

options.A: No interaction, since it is an herbal product
options.B: Higher contraceptive levels and toxicity
options.C: Lower contraceptive levels and failure
options.D: Severe HLA-linked hypersensitivity
options.E: Faster absorption of the contraceptive

items.why: St. John's wort induces CYP3A4, speeding metabolism of drugs such as oral contraceptives, warfarin, and cyclosporine — lowering their levels.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.src: L02 S23; S28 (notes); S30; SG U1-R11
items.stem: In worsening CKD, a renally cleared drug's half-life rises from 6 to 12 hours. About how long will a new steady state take with regular dosing?

options.A: About 24–30 hours
options.B: About 6 hours
options.C: No change, since dose size is unchanged
options.D: About 48–60 hours
options.E: About 12 hours

items.why: Steady state takes about 4–5 half-lives: 4–5 × 12 h = 48–60 h. Clearance ↓ → t½ ↑ → time to steady state ↑ → accumulation risk.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with HIV tests positive for HLA-B*57:01. What does this mean for abacavir?

options.A: Abacavir is contraindicated (hypersensitivity)
options.B: Abacavir will be poorly absorbed
options.C: Abacavir must be given IV only
options.D: Abacavir needs a higher dose
options.E: Abacavir is safe at any dose

items.why: Abacavir is contraindicated in HLA-B*57:01-positive patients because of hypersensitivity — like HLA-B*58:01 with allopurinol.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Before prescribing for a patient who is 10 weeks pregnant, which checklist item directly prompts the PA to reconsider the drug choice?

options.A: The drug's brand and generic names
options.B: Indication — is there a reason to treat?
options.C: Age, pregnancy, and patient-specific factors
options.D: Drug interactions, including CYP450
options.E: Renal and hepatic function

items.why: The checklist: indication; contraindications and allergies; renal and hepatic function; drug interactions (incl. CYP450); age, pregnancy, and other patient-specific factors; correct dose, route, and monitoring.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which narrow-TI drug is about 95% excreted unchanged in urine and essentially not protein-bound?

options.A: Phenytoin
options.B: Warfarin
options.C: Digoxin
options.D: Propranolol
options.E: Lithium

items.why: Lithium: ~95% urinary excretion, 0% protein binding, target ~0.7 mEq/L, toxic above 2 — renal function drives its dosing.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: An IV dose gives 200 mg/L; the half-life is 8 hours. What is the concentration at 24 hours?

options.A: 100 mg/L
options.D: 50 mg/L
options.E: 25 mg/L

items.why: 24 h ÷ 8 h = 3 half-lives: 200 × (1/2)³ = 25 mg/L (87.5% eliminated).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which renal process uses active transporters to move additional drug from blood into the tubule?

options.A: Glomerular filtration
options.B: Biliary excretion
options.C: Ion trapping
options.D: Tubular secretion
options.E: Tubular reabsorption

items.why: Tubular secretion: active transporters move additional drug from blood into the tubule.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: For which drugs does the textbook stress capacity-limited (saturable) elimination?

options.A: Albuterol, insulin, and heparin
options.B: Nitroglycerin, propranolol, and morphine
options.C: Phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin
options.D: Lithium, digoxin, and gentamicin
options.E: Codeine, clopidogrel, and azathioprine

items.why: Capacity-limited elimination (clearance falls as concentration rises) matters for phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin; clearance has no fixed meaning for these drugs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: For a patient with intermediate TPMT activity, how does CPIC guidance adjust a thiopurine such as azathioprine?

options.A: Give the standard dose without monitoring
options.B: Switch to codeine for the same purpose
options.C: Avoid all drugs metabolized by CYP3A4
options.D: Start at double the usual target dose
options.E: Start at about 30–70% of the target dose

items.why: TPMT intermediate activity: start at 30–70% of the target dose and titrate with close monitoring (e.g., white blood cell counts); deficient patients need a drastically reduced dose or an alternative.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient on warfarin and a barbiturate (a CYP inducer) has the barbiturate stopped. What should the PA anticipate?

options.A: Warfarin levels fall, raising clot risk
options.B: Warfarin levels rise, raising bleeding risk
options.C: Warfarin becomes a prodrug once again
options.D: No change, since warfarin is renally cleared
options.E: The barbiturate's effect on CYP persists forever

items.why: Inducers raise warfarin dose needs; stopping the inducer reduces warfarin metabolism, raising plasma levels and causing bleeding.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient overdoses on a weak base. Based on ion trapping, which urine change would speed its excretion?

options.A: Leaving urine pH unchanged
options.B: Making the drug more lipophilic
options.C: Acidifying the urine
options.D: Alkalinizing the urine
options.E: Increasing plasma protein binding

items.why: Weak acids are excreted faster in alkaline urine; weak bases faster in acidic urine — the ionized form is trapped in the tubule and can't be reabsorbed.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Roughly what share of prescription drugs metabolized by the liver does CYP3A4 handle?

options.A: Exactly 100%
options.B: About 25%
options.C: About 5%
options.D: About 10%
options.E: More than 50%

items.why: CYP3A4 alone metabolizes over 50% of the prescription drugs metabolized by the liver — why the lecture's interaction example uses CYP3A4.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why does a large acetaminophen overdose injure the liver?

options.A: Phase II conjugation produces NAPQI
options.B: Overdose induces CYP3A4 in the gut wall
options.C: The kidneys stop excreting the drug
options.D: Glutathione runs out, so NAPQI builds up
options.E: Acetaminophen itself is directly toxic at any dose

items.why: Most acetaminophen is conjugated; a small fraction becomes NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione. In overdose glutathione is depleted and NAPQI injures the liver; N-acetylcysteine within 8–16 h protects.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Theophylline's Vd is 35 L, and the target level is 10 mg/L. Using loading dose = Vd × target, what loading dose is needed?

options.A: 350 mg
options.B: 3.5 mg
options.C: 45 mg
options.D: 35 mg

items.why: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration = 35 L × 10 mg/L = 350 mg — loading doses are based on Vd.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with G6PD deficiency develops very high uric acid during cancer treatment. Which drug does the textbook say is contraindicated?

options.A: Acetaminophen
options.B: Rasburicase
options.C: Allopurinol
options.D: Lithium
options.E: Albuterol

items.why: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (risk of hemolytic anemia); an alternative such as allopurinol is used.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Injury → mediators → nociceptor sensitization → pain.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Musculoskeletal pain is driven by inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines) — NSAIDs and corticosteroids intervene at different points along this cascade.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Corticosteroids = phospholipase A₂ (broad); NSAIDs = COX (prostaglandins).
items.cloze: Corticosteroids = {{c1::phospholipase A₂ (broad)}}; NSAIDs = {{c2::COX (prostaglandins)}}.

items.label: High-yield
items.text: Prostaglandins drive inflammatory pain, and COX makes them.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Nociceptive pain: direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.
items.back: direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.
items.cloze: {{c1::Nociceptive pain}}: direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Inflammatory pain: pain driven by inflammatory mediators.
items.cloze: {{c1::Inflammatory pain}}: pain driven by inflammatory mediators.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Neuropathic pain: pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.
items.back: pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.
items.cloze: {{c1::Neuropathic pain}}: pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Acute pain: recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.
items.back: recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.
items.cloze: {{c1::Acute pain}}: recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.

items.label: Definition
items.text: Chronic pain: persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.
items.back: persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.
items.cloze: {{c1::Chronic pain}}: persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory; pure neuropathic pain belongs to a separate pharmacology unit.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture: NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.
items.front: The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture
items.back: NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.
items.cloze: The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture: {{c1::NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines}}.

items.label: Clinical pearl
items.text: Therapeutic strategies: goal 1 is symptom relief and function (NSAIDs and DMARDs); goal 2 is slowing tissue damage, for which DMARDs are absolutely necessary. Response is tracked with indices such as DAS28 in RA.
items.back: goal 1 is symptom relief and function (NSAIDs and DMARDs); goal 2 is slowing tissue damage, for which DMARDs are absolutely necessary. Response is tracked with indices such as DAS28 in RA.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: Corticosteroids act upstream at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.

items.label: Exam trap
items.text: The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.
items.back: release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.
items.cloze: Tissue injury → {{c1::release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Key mediators: prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).
items.back: prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).
items.cloze: Key mediators: {{c1::prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6)}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation: the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections.
items.front: Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation
items.back: the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections.
items.cloze: Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation: {{c1::the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections}}.

items.label: How it works
items.text: NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors act at the COX step; glucocorticoids act further upstream; cytokine inhibitors and analgesics act through separate, parallel pathways.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂ (membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.
items.back: arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.
items.cloze: {{c1::Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂}} (membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Nociceptor sensitization: injury releases PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines, which lower the pain threshold — normally harmless stimuli now hurt.
items.back: injury releases PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines, which lower the pain threshold — normally harmless stimuli now hurt.
items.cloze: {{c1::Nociceptor sensitization}}: injury releases PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines, which {{c2::lower the pain threshold}} — normally harmless stimuli now hurt.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Prostaglandins sensitize nociceptors, so they are the main NSAID target; bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines are not blocked by NSAIDs.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Where drugs act: NSAIDs block COX; corticosteroids block PLA2 (phospholipase A₂) one step upstream.
items.back: NSAIDs block COX; corticosteroids block PLA2 (phospholipase A₂) one step upstream.
items.cloze: Where drugs act: {{c1::NSAIDs block COX}}; corticosteroids block PLA2 (phospholipase A₂) one step upstream.

items.label: How it works
items.text: The immune response: chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.
items.back: chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.
items.cloze: {{c1::The immune response}}: chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.

items.label: How it works
items.text: The lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid makes leukotrienes (chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability) — a separate branch from the COX step NSAIDs block.

items.label: Example
items.text: Corticosteroids (block phospholipase A₂) vs. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors (block COX): two distinct points of intervention.
items.cloze: Corticosteroids (block phospholipase A₂) vs. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors (block COX): {{c1::two distinct points of intervention}}.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why are corticosteroids broader than NSAIDs? They act at phospholipase A₂, before arachidonic acid is released, so every mediator made from it falls — NSAIDs only stop the COX branch.
items.front: Why are corticosteroids broader than NSAIDs?

items.text: Acetaminophen treats pain and fever but is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent; its overdose toxicity is mediated by NAPQI accumulation.

items.text: Acetaminophen is central, with no real anti-inflammatory effect. Overdose means NAPQI, and the antidote is NAC.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why does N-acetylcysteine work? Glutathione is what safely conjugates NAPQI. Overdose uses it up; N-acetylcysteine is a glutathione precursor, so it refills the supply.
items.back: Glutathione is what safely conjugates NAPQI. Overdose uses it up; N-acetylcysteine is a glutathione precursor, so it refills the supply.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why do NSAIDs hurt the stomach and kidney? Blocking COX-1, the housekeeping enzyme, removes the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa and keep renal blood flow normal.
items.front: Why do NSAIDs hurt the stomach and kidney?

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why the “triple whammy”? An ACE inhibitor/ARB, a diuretic, and an NSAID each push kidney perfusion the wrong way at once — together they cause acute kidney injury.
items.back: An ACE inhibitor/ARB, a diuretic, and an NSAID each push kidney perfusion the wrong way at once — together they cause acute kidney injury.

items.text: DMARDs (conventional and biologic — methotrexate, adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, tocilizumab, rituximab, abatacept) modify RA’s disease course rather than only masking symptoms.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why can’t RA be treated like OA? RA is immune-mediated joint destruction; analgesics ease pain but leave the immune attack — and the damage — running.
items.front: Why can’t RA be treated like OA?
items.back: RA is immune-mediated joint destruction; analgesics ease pain but leave the immune attack — and the damage — running.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Methotrexate rules = W-F-P: Weekly (never daily), Folate with it, Pregnancy contraindicated.
items.back: Weekly (never daily), Folate with it, Pregnancy contraindicated.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Methotrexate toxicity hits L-B-L: Liver, Bone marrow, Lung.

items.label: Memory hook
items.text: Why screen for TB and hepatitis first? These drugs suppress the immune response that keeps latent infections in check, so a hidden infection can reactivate.
items.front: Why screen for TB and hepatitis first?
items.back: These drugs suppress the immune response that keeps latent infections in check, so a hidden infection can reactivate.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 1, corticosteroids are shown blocking the pathway at the "Membrane Phospholipids → Arachidonic Acid" step, while NSAIDs act one step later. What does this positioning explain?

options.A: Corticosteroids act upstream of NSAIDs, which is why they can suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators, not just prostaglandins
options.B: Corticosteroids and NSAIDs block the exact same enzyme
options.C: NSAIDs act upstream of corticosteroids
options.D: Neither drug class affects the arachidonic acid pathway

items.why: By inhibiting phospholipase A₂, corticosteroids block the release of arachidonic acid itself — upstream of COX — which is why they suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators (not just prostaglandins) than NSAIDs, which act only at the COX step.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which mediator is the primary target of NSAID therapy within the inflammatory pain pathway?

options.A: Prostaglandins
options.B: Histamine
options.C: Bradykinin
options.D: Cytokines broadly (e.g., all of TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6)

items.why: NSAIDs inhibit COX enzymes, directly reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Histamine, bradykinin, and cytokines are important inflammatory mediators too, but they are not the primary target of NSAID mechanism.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, hepatotoxicity results primarily from which mechanism?

options.A: Direct COX inhibition in the liver
options.B: Excess Phase II glucuronidation
options.C: Accumulation of NAPQI after glutathione stores are depleted
options.D: Renal crystal formation

items.why: NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione, accumulates once glutathione stores are exhausted in overdose, causing hepatocyte injury — which is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Based on Figure 2, a patient with a history of GI ulcer but no cardiovascular disease is switched from ibuprofen to celecoxib. What is the most likely net effect on this patient’s risk profile?

options.A: Lower GI risk, with some increase in cardiovascular risk
options.B: Both GI and cardiovascular risk decrease
options.C: No change in either risk, since all NSAIDs carry identical risk profiles
options.D: Both GI and cardiovascular risk increase

items.why: Figure 2 shows celecoxib’s illustrative GI-risk bar is lower than the nonselective NSAID bar, while its cardiovascular-risk bar is higher — exactly the trade-off described in the celecoxib bullet slide. For this GI-ulcer-history patient without cardiovascular disease, that trade may be favorable, but the increased cardiovascular risk should still be discussed.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with CKD, hypertension, and anticoagulant use needs analgesia for osteoarthritis. Which class carries the highest combined renal and bleeding risk for this patient?

options.A: Acetaminophen
options.B: Oral NSAIDs
options.C: Topical capsaicin
options.D: Physical therapy alone

items.why: This patient has multiple NSAID red flags at once: CKD (renal risk), anticoagulant use (bleeding risk), and hypertension (cardiovascular risk) — oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk here.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In Figure 3, which biologic DMARD acts earliest in the cascade shown, before cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6 are even released?

options.A: Adalimumab
options.B: Tocilizumab
options.C: Abatacept
options.D: Rituximab

items.why: Abatacept blocks T-cell costimulation — the step furthest upstream in the diagram, occurring before activated T cells drive cytokine release (blocked downstream by adalimumab/tocilizumab) or B-cell activity (blocked by rituximab).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which feature distinguishes a DMARD from an NSAID in the management of rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: DMARDs provide faster pain relief than NSAIDs
options.B: NSAIDs suppress the immune system more potently than DMARDs
options.C: DMARDs modify the underlying disease process rather than only masking symptoms
options.D: DMARDs are only available as biologic agents

items.why: An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing RA’s disease trajectory; a DMARD (conventional or biologic) is intended to slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation itself.

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, why is N-acetylcysteine effective?

options.A: It speeds renal excretion of unchanged acetaminophen
options.B: It is a glutathione precursor that restores NAPQI detoxification
options.C: It blocks COX in the liver and lowers prostaglandin levels
options.D: It inhibits the enzyme that forms NAPQI from the drug
options.E: It binds acetaminophen in the gut and prevents absorption

items.why: Overdose depletes glutathione so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI (S19; SG U2-R3).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 40-year-old with an acutely swollen, inflamed knee asks for the drug that best treats the inflammation itself. Why is acetaminophen not the best choice?

options.A: It only works when given intravenously in hospital
options.B: It causes more GI bleeding than the NSAIDs do
options.C: It is contraindicated in anyone with joint swelling
options.D: Its anti-inflammatory effect at the periphery is minimal
options.E: It has no analgesic effect in musculoskeletal pain

items.why: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever centrally, but its peripheral anti-inflammatory effect is minimal — it is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent (S15).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which statement best explains why nonselective NSAIDs cause GI and renal adverse effects?

options.A: They block TNF-α, which normally protects the stomach lining
options.B: They block phospholipase A₂ and stop all mediator release
options.C: They inhibit COX-1, which protects gastric mucosa and renal blood flow
options.D: They inhibit COX-2, the only source of protective prostaglandins
options.E: They deplete glutathione, which injures the gut and kidney

items.why: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects (S26; SG U2-R4).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) and hydrochlorothiazide starts daily naproxen for knee pain. Two weeks later, creatinine has risen sharply. What pattern explains this?

options.A: Expected COX-2 renal protection failing under stress
options.B: Bleeding from the NSAID plus the ACE inhibitor together
options.C: The “triple whammy”: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic causing AKI
options.D: A GI ulcer from NSAID plus diuretic, causing dehydration
options.E: Hepatotoxicity from NAPQI formed by naproxen metabolism

items.why: NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise AKI risk, and adding a diuretic is the high-yield “triple whammy” AKI pattern (S36; S36 notes).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which nonselective NSAID does the lecture restrict to short-term use because of significant GI and renal risk?

options.A: Ketorolac
options.B: Ibuprofen
options.C: Diclofenac
options.D: Celecoxib
options.E: Naproxen

items.why: Ketorolac is for short-term use only because of significant GI/renal risk (S28).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient takes low-dose aspirin for cardioprotection and starts regular ibuprofen for back pain. What is the textbook concern?

options.A: Ibuprofen converts aspirin to the toxic metabolite NAPQI
options.B: Ibuprofen speeds aspirin’s renal excretion fivefold
options.C: Ibuprofen blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition
options.D: Aspirin makes ibuprofen COX-2 selective, raising CV risk
options.E: Both drugs together protect the kidney from injury

items.why: Concomitant ibuprofen antagonizes aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect (p. 680).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 66-year-old has knee pain worse with activity, no systemic symptoms, and mild disease. Which first-line drug does the lecture call reasonable?

options.A: Acetaminophen for mild osteoarthritis pain
options.B: Methotrexate to slow joint destruction
options.C: Hydroxychloroquine for mild disease
options.D: Adalimumab to block TNF-α signaling
options.E: Ketorolac taken daily as maintenance

items.why: Acetaminophen is a reasonable first-line for mild OA pain (S43).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: What is the key difference in treatment goals between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: Both aim only at pain relief with NSAIDs
options.B: OA aims at cartilage regrowth with DMARDs
options.C: OA aims at pain and function; RA aims to suppress disease activity
options.D: OA aims to suppress immunity; RA aims at pain relief only
options.E: RA aims at weight loss; OA aims at infection control

items.why: OA treatment targets pain control and function; RA treatment must suppress disease activity, not just pain (S41).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient newly started on methotrexate for RA asks whether to take a tablet every morning “to keep levels steady.” What is the correct counseling?

options.A: Take it daily but skip the folate supplement
options.B: Take it only on days when joints are painful
options.C: Take it twice daily, like naproxen, for steady levels
options.D: Take it once weekly, because daily dosing can be fatal
options.E: Take it daily with food to reduce stomach upset

items.why: Methotrexate is dosed weekly, not daily — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal (S49; SG U2-R7).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: What is methotrexate’s mechanism as taught in the lecture, and what is co-prescribed to reduce its toxicity?

options.A: COX-2 inhibition; a proton pump inhibitor
options.B: Phospholipase A₂ blockade; calcium supplementation
options.C: TNF-α blockade; tuberculosis screening
options.D: Glutathione depletion; N-acetylcysteine
options.E: Dihydrofolate reductase inhibition; folate supplementation

items.why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses; folate is routinely co-prescribed (S49; SG U2-R7; SG U2-M).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A 29-year-old with active RA who is planning a pregnancy needs a DMARD. Which drug from the lecture is contraindicated?

options.A: Celecoxib, because it is a disease-modifying drug
options.B: Sulfasalazine, because it is only used alone
options.C: Acetaminophen, because it is a DMARD
options.D: Methotrexate, because it is teratogenic
options.E: Hydroxychloroquine, because of its poor safety profile

items.why: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic (S49).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Before starting adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis, which baseline step does the lecture specifically call for?

options.A: Screening for tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C
options.B: Starting folate to prevent bone marrow toxicity
options.C: Adding an ACE inhibitor to protect the kidney
options.D: Checking for all hidden acetaminophen sources
options.E: Avoiding all vaccines until therapy has begun

items.why: Biologics cause immunosuppression; baseline tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening comes before starting them (S56).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient on a biologic DMARD calls with a fever of 38.6 °C and a productive cough. What lecture principle drives the advice to be seen promptly?

options.A: NSAID-like renal toxicity makes fever dangerous
options.B: Fever means the biologic is working as intended
options.C: Immunosuppression raises infection risk across all DMARDs
options.D: Biologics raise cardiovascular risk like celecoxib
options.E: Biologics cause hidden acetaminophen overdose

items.why: The major safety theme across all DMARDs is immunosuppression → increased infection risk; patients should report fevers or infection symptoms promptly (S56; SG U2-R8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Match the drug to its target: which pairing is correct?

options.A: Abatacept — B-lymphocyte depletion
options.B: Tocilizumab — IL-6 receptor signaling
options.C: Etanercept — IL-6 receptor signaling
options.D: Adalimumab — T-cell costimulation
options.E: Rituximab — TNF-α signaling

items.why: Tocilizumab is the lecture’s IL-6 inhibitor (S51; SG U2-R8).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: A patient with RA and high cardiovascular risk is being considered for tofacitinib. Which boxed warning applies to all JAK inhibitors?

options.A: Lymphoma only, exactly the same as the TNF inhibitors
options.B: Teratogenicity that requires strict weekly-only dosing
options.C: Retinopathy that requires annual eye examinations
options.D: Venous thromboembolism, major cardiovascular events, and cancer
options.E: Fatal hepatotoxicity from NAPQI accumulating in the liver

items.why: All JAK inhibitors carry an FDA boxed warning for VTE (DVT, PE), MACE, and cancer (p. 686).

items.label: Self-test question
items.stem: Which conventional DMARD requires a baseline eye exam and annual screening after 5 years because of retinopathy?

options.A: Methotrexate
options.B: Mycophenolate mofetil
options.C: Sulfasalazine
options.D: Leflunomide
options.E: Hydroxychloroquine

items.why: Antimalarials bind melanin-rich tissue such as the retina; a baseline exam and annual screening after 5 years are recommended (p. 684).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Per the textbook, which instruction about ketorolac is correct?

options.A: Start therapy with an oral dose
options.B: Maximum daily dose is 240 mg
options.C: Use no longer than 5 days
options.D: Double the dose in patients over 65
options.E: Safe long-term in renal impairment

items.why: Ketorolac is for short-term use only (slides); the textbook adds a 120 mg/day maximum, halved doses in older, light, or renally impaired patients, and no more than 5 days.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient from a region with high tuberculosis rates is about to start adalimumab. Which step matters most before the first dose?

options.A: Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C
options.B: Obtain a baseline eye examination
options.C: Review labels for hidden acetaminophen
options.D: Check a uric acid level
options.E: Start folate supplementation

items.why: Immunosuppression is the shared DMARD risk; baseline TB and hepatitis B/C screening comes before biologics (TNF inhibitors can reactivate TB and hepatitis B).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Why is celecoxib associated with more cardiovascular events than its GI profile would suggest?

options.A: It raises renal blood flow excessively
options.B: TXA2 falls while PGI2 is preserved
options.C: It depletes glutathione in the heart
options.D: PGI2 falls while platelet TXA2 is preserved
options.E: It blocks COX-1 more than COX-2

items.why: Celecoxib blocks COX-2, lowering prostacyclin (PGI2) without a matching drop in platelet thromboxane (TXA2, made by spared COX-1) — the balance tips toward clotting.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which drug is a TNF inhibitor?

options.A: Abatacept
options.B: Leflunomide
options.C: Etanercept
options.D: Tocilizumab
options.E: Rituximab

items.why: Adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximab are the lecture's TNF inhibitors.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which NSAID is noted for oral and topical formulations?

options.A: Diclofenac
options.B: Indomethacin
options.C: Ketorolac
options.D: Naproxen
options.E: Celecoxib

items.why: Diclofenac is available in oral and topical formulations; topical NSAIDs give local relief with much lower systemic exposure.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with RA on adalimumab has a family history of lymphoma and asks about cancer risk. Which statement matches the textbook?

options.A: Boxed warnings apply only to IV biologics
options.B: TNF inhibitors lower lymphoma risk to zero
options.C: Only methotrexate carries a malignancy warning
options.D: Cancer risk applies only to JAK inhibitors
options.E: TNF inhibitors carry a boxed malignancy warning

items.why: The FDA placed a boxed warning on all anti-TNF agents about possible malignancy, especially lymphoma; periodic skin exams are advised.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: What defines a drug as “disease-modifying” in rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: It slows or halts joint destruction
options.B: It selectively blocks the COX-2 isoform
options.C: It relieves pain faster than NSAIDs
options.D: It is given only as an injection
options.E: It lowers fever through the hypothalamus

items.why: A DMARD is intended to alter the course of RA — slowing or halting joint destruction and systemic inflammation — rather than only masking symptoms.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 19-year-old arrives 4 hours after taking a large acetaminophen overdose. Which drug restores the pathway that detoxifies the toxic metabolite?

options.A: Leucovorin
options.B: Naloxone
options.C: N-acetylcysteine
options.D: Folic acid
options.E: Omeprazole

items.why: Overdose depletes glutathione, so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine is a glutathione precursor that replenishes it to detoxify NAPQI.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which non-drug approaches does the lecture include in osteoarthritis management?

options.A: Fasting, high-protein diet, bed rest
options.B: Glutathione replenishment, label review
options.C: Live vaccines, TB screening, folate
options.D: Activity modification, physical therapy, weight management
options.E: Nerve ablation, spinal cord stimulation

items.why: OA management includes activity modification, physical therapy, and weight management alongside drugs.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A woman in her third trimester asks whether she can take naproxen for back pain. Based on the lecture, what is the best response?

options.A: Use ketorolac daily as a long-term option
options.B: Use it freely — NSAIDs are safest in late pregnancy
options.C: Use celecoxib instead — COX-2 drugs are exempt
options.D: Add folate to make naproxen safe
options.E: Avoid it — late pregnancy is an NSAID caution

items.why: The lecture lists late pregnancy among the conditions to use NSAIDs with caution or avoid.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient will start infliximab next month and is due for a live vaccine. When should the vaccine be given?

options.A: One week after the first infusion
options.B: Never — vaccines are banned for life
options.C: Only if a fever develops on therapy
options.D: Before infliximab is started
options.E: Any time, since biologics don't affect immunity

items.why: Update vaccines — especially live vaccines — before starting DMARD therapy, because these drugs suppress the immune response.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which sequence describes how tissue injury produces musculoskeletal pain?

options.A: Injury → mediator release → nociceptor sensitization → pain
options.B: Injury → glutathione loss → NAPQI build-up → pain
options.C: Injury → nerve transection → cortical atrophy → pain
options.D: Injury → T-cell depletion → B-cell surge → pain
options.E: Injury → COX-1 induction → gastric protection → pain

items.why: Tissue injury releases inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines) that sensitize nociceptors, producing pain.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 22-year-old took a single large acetaminophen ingestion at a known time; a level drawn 8 hours later is 120 mcg/mL. Using the lecture's nomogram, what is the next step?

options.A: Wait until 24 hours for a second level first
options.B: Start NAC: the level is above the treatment line
options.C: Ignore the level and treat with an NSAID
options.D: Discharge: levels fall below 150 by 8 hours
options.E: Repeat the level before 4 hours have passed

items.why: On the Rumack-Matthew nomogram the slide's example — 8 h, 120 mcg/mL — is above the treatment line, so NAC is started (give early for best effect).

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with RA cannot tolerate methotrexate. Which conventional DMARD does the lecture name as the alternative?

options.A: Sulfasalazine
options.B: Leflunomide
options.C: Rituximab
options.D: Hydroxychloroquine
options.E: Celecoxib

items.why: Leflunomide is the alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use who has barely eaten for days takes acetaminophen at the upper end of normal dosing. Why is their liver risk higher?

options.A: Lower glutathione plus induced CYP2E1 makes more NAPQI
options.B: Fasting speeds renal excretion of the parent drug
options.C: Alcohol blocks COX in the liver, adding NSAID toxicity
options.D: Fasting saturates TXA2, causing hepatic bleeding
options.E: Alcohol converts acetaminophen into an NSAID

items.why: Chronic alcohol use and fasting lower glutathione (GSH) and both induce CYP2E1, so more drug becomes NAPQI and less can be neutralized.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: Which statement correctly describes COX-1?

options.A: Main source of inflammatory prostaglandins
options.B: Target of celecoxib's selective inhibition
options.C: Enzyme that converts acetaminophen to NAPQI
options.D: Inducible enzyme found mainly at inflamed sites
options.E: Housekeeping enzyme protecting stomach and renal flow

items.why: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A 70-year-old with knee OA has a flare limited to one knee despite acetaminophen and topical diclofenac. Which option does the lecture list for short-term relief?

options.A: High-dose hydroxychloroquine
options.B: Daily ketorolac for a month
options.C: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
options.D: Infliximab infusion
options.E: Weekly oral methotrexate

items.why: Intra-articular corticosteroid injections give short-term relief for flares in a single joint.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A patient with heart failure on furosemide develops worsening edema after starting high-dose ibuprofen. What best explains this?

options.A: Ibuprofen is COX-2 selective and hurts the heart
options.B: Furosemide blocks ibuprofen's COX inhibition
options.C: The edema is NAPQI-induced liver failure
options.D: NSAIDs cause fluid retention and blunt diuretics
options.E: Ibuprofen is a CYP inducer lowering furosemide

items.why: NSAIDs cause renal fluid retention and, with diuretics, reduce the diuretic effect and raise renal risk; heart failure is a caution for NSAID use.

items.label: Practice-exam question
items.stem: A prescription reads infliximab. What does the stem “-ximab” tell you?
